label: The Tseitin encoding
prereqs: Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms
lesson:
# The Tseitin encoding

SAT solvers read conjunctive normal form, but designs arrive as circuits. The Tseitin encoding bridges the two: it gives every gate output a fresh variable and writes a few clauses that force that variable to equal the gate's function. The result is linear in the circuit size and equisatisfiable with it. Every SAT-based engine in this course, from equivalence checking to bounded model checking, starts by building this CNF, so its size is the first number a tool designer estimates.

## Clauses for one gate

For $y = a \wedge b$ the encoding writes $y \leftrightarrow (a \wedge b)$ as three clauses: $(\neg y \vee a)$, $(\neg y \vee b)$ and $(y \vee \neg a \vee \neg b)$. The two binary clauses say that $y$ true forces each input true; the long clause says that both inputs true force $y$ true. A $k$-input AND therefore costs $k$ binary clauses plus one clause of $k + 1$ literals, so $k + 1$ clauses. OR is the dual: $(y \vee \neg a_i)$ for each input and $(\neg y \vee a_1 \vee \dots \vee a_k)$, again $k + 1$ clauses. NAND and NOR only flip the polarity of $y$. A 2-input XOR $y = a \oplus b$ needs one 3-literal clause per row of its truth table: $(\neg y \vee a \vee b)$, $(\neg y \vee \neg a \vee \neg b)$, $(y \vee \neg a \vee b)$, $(y \vee a \vee \neg b)$, so 4 clauses. A NOT gate gets no variable at all: its readers use the negated literal of its input.

## Counting a whole circuit

Under this convention a circuit's CNF has one variable per primary input and one per non-inverter gate, and its clauses are the sum of the per-gate costs plus one unit clause asserting the output (or the miter, or the bad signal). Take 4 inputs, two 2-input AND gates, one 3-input OR gate, one XOR gate and one NOT gate. Variables: $4 + 4 = 8$, since the NOT adds none. Clauses: $3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 15$. The count is linear in the number of gates, which is the whole point: a netlist with a million gates becomes a CNF with a few million clauses, well within reach of a modern solver. The encoding is equisatisfiable, not equivalent: every satisfying assignment of the circuit extends uniquely to the gate variables, and every model of the CNF restricted to the inputs is a satisfying input vector.

## Why new variables pay off

Without new variables, a CNF over the inputs alone can be exponentially large. The parity $x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus x_n = 1$ is false on the $2^{n-1}$ even-parity rows, and any clause over these variables that is implied by parity must mention all $n$ of them, so it excludes exactly one row. The smallest direct CNF therefore has $2^{n-1}$ clauses. A Tseitin chain of $n - 1$ two-input XORs costs $4(n - 1)$ clauses plus one unit clause, $4n - 3$ in total. For $n = 8$ that is 29 clauses against 128, and the gap doubles with every input. Production encoders go further: the Plaisted-Greenbaum variant keeps only the clauses needed for the polarity in which each gate is used, and AIG-based tools such as ABC encode only AND nodes, with inverters on edges.

## Going deeper

Biere, Heule, van Maaren and Walsh (eds.), "Handbook of Satisfiability" (2nd ed., 2021), the chapter on CNF encodings; Kroening and Strichman, "Decision Procedures" (2nd ed., 2016), chapter 1.

label: Unit propagation
lesson:
# Unit propagation

Unit propagation, also called Boolean constraint propagation, is the inference step that every SAT solver runs after every assignment. When all literals of a clause but one are false, that last literal must be true. Repeating this until nothing changes either extends the assignment or exposes a conflict. Solvers spend most of their run time here, so its rules and its cost model shape the design of the whole solver.

## Unit clauses

Under a partial assignment, a clause is satisfied if some literal is true, conflicting if every literal is false, unit if every literal but one is false and that one is unassigned, and unresolved otherwise. Only unit clauses force anything. Take $(x_1 \vee \neg x_2 \vee x_3)$ with $x_1 = 0$ and $x_3 = 0$: two literals are false and $\neg x_2$ is unassigned, so the clause is unit and forces $x_2 = 0$. With only $x_1 = 0$ it is unresolved, because two literals are still free. With $x_3 = 1$ it is satisfied and plays no further role until backtracking. To count the unit clauses of a CNF under an assignment, scan each clause, skip it if any literal is true, and mark it unit when exactly one literal is unassigned.

## Propagating to a fixpoint

Propagation repeats: set the forced literal of every unit clause, which may make new clauses unit, until no unit clause remains or some clause is conflicting. Take $(x_1)$, $(\neg x_1 \vee x_2)$, $(\neg x_2 \vee \neg x_3)$, $(x_3 \vee x_4 \vee x_5)$ and $(\neg x_4 \vee x_5)$. The unit clause sets $x_1 = 1$; then $(\neg x_1 \vee x_2)$ forces $x_2 = 1$; then $(\neg x_2 \vee \neg x_3)$ forces $x_3 = 0$. Now $(x_3 \vee x_4 \vee x_5)$ has two free literals and $(\neg x_4 \vee x_5)$ has two, so the fixpoint assigns three variables. The fixpoint does not depend on the order in which unit clauses are processed, as long as no conflict arises; if one does, the solver stops and analyzes it. Propagation alone decides satisfiability for Horn formulas, but in general it is only a cheap, sound inference that leaves the rest to search.

## Propagation after a decision

Inside search, propagation runs after every decision, and the literals it sets are the decision's implications. Decide $x_1 = 0$ on $(x_1 \vee x_2)$, $(\neg x_2 \vee x_3)$, $(x_1 \vee \neg x_3 \vee x_4)$ and $(\neg x_4 \vee \neg x_5)$. The first clause forces $x_2 = 1$, the second $x_3 = 1$, the third (with $x_1 = 0$ and $x_3 = 1$) forces $x_4 = 1$, and the last forces $x_5 = 0$: four implied variables from one decision. This chain is what the implication graph records, and the reason clause of each implied literal is the clause that became unit. Because propagation dominates run time, solvers avoid rescanning every clause: the two-watched-literal scheme visits a clause only when one of two chosen literals becomes false.

## Going deeper

Biere et al. (eds.), "Handbook of Satisfiability" (2nd ed., 2021), the chapter on CDCL solvers; Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang and Malik, "Chaff: Engineering an Efficient SAT Solver" (DAC 2001).

label: DPLL
lesson:
# DPLL

DPLL, named for Davis, Putnam, Logemann and Loveland, is the backtracking search at the heart of every complete SAT solver. It picks a variable, tries a value, propagates, and backtracks on a conflict. Modern CDCL solvers add learning and non-chronological backtracking, but their skeleton is still DPLL. Tracing it by hand on small formulas is the best way to see why plain backtracking repeats work and what learning removes.

## Split, propagate, backtrack

DPLL is the Shannon expansion turned into search: $F$ is satisfiable if $F|_{x=0}$ or $F|_{x=1}$ is. The convention used here: after every assignment run unit propagation; report SAT as soon as every clause is satisfied; otherwise branch on the lowest-index unassigned variable, try 0 first, and on a conflict undo back to the most recent decision whose other value is untried (chronological backtracking). A decision is every branching assignment, including the second value tried after a backtrack; forced values are not decisions. On $(x_1 \vee x_2)$, $(x_1 \vee \neg x_2)$, $(\neg x_1 \vee x_3)$: decide $x_1 = 0$ (decision 1); the first clause forces $x_2 = 1$ and the second then conflicts. Backtrack and set $x_1 = 1$ (decision 2); propagation forces $x_3 = 1$ and every clause is satisfied. Two decisions, answer SAT.

## Counting decisions on a satisfiable formula

Take $C_1 = (x_1 \vee x_2 \vee x_3)$, $C_2 = (x_1 \vee \neg x_2)$, $C_3 = (\neg x_3 \vee x_4)$, $C_4 = (x_1 \vee x_2 \vee \neg x_4)$. Decide $x_1 = 0$ (decision 1). $C_2$ forces $x_2 = 0$, then $C_1$ forces $x_3 = 1$, $C_3$ forces $x_4 = 1$, and $C_4$ has every literal false: conflict. Backtrack: $x_1 = 1$ (decision 2) satisfies $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_4$, but $C_3$ is unresolved and nothing is unit. Branch on $x_2 = 0$ (decision 3): $C_3$ is still open. Branch on $x_3 = 0$ (decision 4): $C_3$ is satisfied, so every clause is, and the solver reports SAT after 4 decisions. Two of those decisions were on variables that did not matter once $x_1 = 1$; real solvers waste effort the same way, which is one reason decision heuristics prefer variables in recent conflicts.

## Proving unsatisfiability

To answer UNSAT, DPLL must refute both values of every branch: the search tree is explored completely and every leaf ends in a conflict. With $(x_1 \vee x_2)$, $(x_1 \vee \neg x_2)$, $(\neg x_1 \vee x_2)$, $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_2)$: decide $x_1 = 0$ (decision 1); the first two clauses force $x_2 = 1$ and $x_2 = 0$, a conflict. Decide $x_1 = 1$ (decision 2); the last two clauses conflict the same way. With both values of the first variable refuted, the formula is UNSAT after 2 decisions. In general the tree can be exponential, and a DPLL refutation corresponds to a tree-like resolution proof, which is provably weaker than the general resolution proofs that clause learning can produce. That gap is why every competitive solver is CDCL.

## Going deeper

Davis, Logemann and Loveland, "A Machine Program for Theorem-Proving" (Communications of the ACM, 1962); Biere et al. (eds.), "Handbook of Satisfiability" (2nd ed., 2021), the chapters on complete algorithms and CDCL.

label: Implication graphs and decision levels
lesson:
# Implication graphs and decision levels

When a CDCL solver hits a conflict it needs to know why. The implication graph records the answer: one node per assigned literal, edges from the literals that forced an implication, and decision levels that say when each literal was set. Conflict analysis, clause learning and backjumping are all walks over this graph, so reading it fluently is the prerequisite for everything that makes modern solvers fast.

## Decision levels

Each decision opens a new decision level: the first decision is at level 1, the next at level 2, and so on; literals forced before any decision are at level 0. An implied literal sits at the highest level among the literals that forced it, which is the level of the most recent decision when propagation set it. Suppose $x_1 = 1$ is decided at level 1 and $x_4 = 0$ at level 2. If $x_7 = 1$ is implied by $(\neg x_1 \vee x_4 \vee x_7)$, its antecedents are $x_1$ (level 1) and $x_4$ (level 2), so $x_7$ is at level 2. If $x_9 = 0$ is implied by $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_9)$, its only antecedent is at level 1, so $x_9$ is at level 1. When implications are listed out of order, compute levels recursively: first the literals whose antecedents are all decisions, then those that depend on them.

## Nodes, edges and reasons

Every assigned literal is a node. A decision has no incoming edges. An implied literal $\ell$ has a reason clause, the clause that became unit and forced it, of the form $(\ell \vee \neg a_1 \vee \dots \vee \neg a_m)$, where each $a_i$ is a literal that was already true. The graph has an edge from each $a_i$ to $\ell$, so the in-degree of $\ell$ equals the size of its reason clause minus one. If $x_5 = 1$ is implied by $(x_5 \vee \neg x_2 \vee x_3 \vee \neg x_8)$, the antecedents are $x_2 = 1$, $x_3 = 0$ and $x_8 = 1$, and the node $x_5$ has three incoming edges. Because propagation only uses literals that are already set, the graph is acyclic, and the trail order of assignment is a topological order of it. Solvers store the graph implicitly: each variable keeps a pointer to its reason clause and its level.

## The conflict and its cone

A conflict adds a special node $\kappa$ with an edge from the negation of each literal of the falsified clause. Walking backwards from $\kappa$ through reason clauses gives the conflict's backward cone. The decisions inside it are a cause of the conflict: setting them the same way always reproduces it. Their negations form a valid learned clause, the all-decision cut. Suppose decisions $x_1 = 1$ (level 1), $x_4 = 0$ (level 2) and $x_6 = 1$ (level 3) are made, and walking back from the conflict reaches $x_1$ and $x_6$ but not $x_4$. The decision clause is $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_6)$, two literals, and it already says level 2 was irrelevant. Cutting the graph closer to the conflict, at a unique implication point, usually gives a shorter and more useful clause, which is the next concept.

## Going deeper

label: Conflict-driven clause learning
lesson:
# Conflict-driven clause learning

Conflict-driven clause learning turned SAT from a theoretical hardness example into an industrial engine that routinely solves formulas with millions of clauses from hardware verification. CDCL keeps the DPLL skeleton of decide and propagate, but on every conflict it analyzes the implication graph, learns a new clause, and jumps back past irrelevant decisions. Knowing the loop, why the learned clauses are sound, and how solvers keep them under control is the base for every SAT-based tool.

## The CDCL loop

A CDCL solver repeats one loop. Decide: pick an unassigned variable and a value, opening a new decision level. Propagate: run unit propagation to a fixpoint. If no conflict arises and every variable is assigned, report SAT with the current assignment. If a conflict arises at level 0, report UNSAT, because level-0 literals are forced by the formula alone. Otherwise analyze the conflict: walk the implication graph back to the first unique implication point and derive a learned clause. Add the clause, backjump to the second-highest decision level in it, and let propagation use it: after the backjump the learned clause is unit, so it immediately asserts the negation of the UIP literal. Restarts occasionally clear the trail back to level 0 without forgetting learned clauses. Each piece (decision heuristic, analysis, backjump, restart, deletion) is its own concept in this subdomain.

## Why learned clauses are sound and useful

Conflict analysis is a sequence of resolution steps. Starting from the falsified clause, it resolves with the reason clause of a literal assigned at the conflict level, and repeats. Every resolvent is implied by the clauses it came from, so the learned clause is implied by the original formula: adding it never removes a model, and the answer cannot change. What it changes is the search. DPLL that fails below $x_1 = 1$ and $x_4 = 0$ will happily make the same assignment again in another branch and rediscover the same conflict. A learned clause such as $(\neg x_1 \vee x_4)$ blocks that combination everywhere in the remaining search. Because every learned clause is a resolution consequence, the sequence of learned clauses ending in the empty clause is a proof of unsatisfiability that an independent checker can verify by reverse unit propagation, which is what the DRAT proof format records.

## Managing the learned-clause database

A solver can learn a clause per conflict and run millions of conflicts, so learned clauses would soon dominate memory and slow propagation, since every clause sits on two watch lists. Solvers therefore delete learned clauses periodically. They can delete only learned clauses: those are redundant consequences, whereas deleting an original clause could change the problem. To choose what to keep, modern solvers measure the literal block distance (LBD), the number of distinct decision levels among a clause's literals when it was learned; clauses with small LBD, often called glue clauses, tend to keep propagating and are kept, while others are kept only if recently active. A solver asked for an auditable UNSAT answer also logs its learned clauses and deletions as a DRAT proof, so that a small, separately trusted checker can confirm the result without trusting the solver.

## Going deeper

Marques-Silva, Lynce and Malik, "Conflict-Driven Clause Learning SAT Solvers", in Biere et al. (eds.), "Handbook of Satisfiability" (2nd ed., 2021); Audemard and Simon, "Predicting Learnt Clauses Quality in Modern SAT Solvers" (IJCAI 2009); Een and Sorensson, "An Extensible SAT-solver" (SAT 2003), the MiniSat paper.

label: First-UIP learned clauses
lesson:
# First-UIP learned clauses

When propagation hits a conflict, the solver has many valid clauses it could learn. The first-UIP scheme picks one with a precise recipe: resolve backwards from the conflict until exactly one literal of the conflict level remains. It is the scheme used by essentially every CDCL solver, because the clause it produces is short, asserting after backjumping, and cheap to compute from the trail. Computing it by hand is the core skill of conflict analysis.

## Unique implication points

Look at the implication graph restricted to the conflict level. A unique implication point (UIP) is a node of that level through which every path from the level's decision to the conflict passes. The decision itself is always a UIP, the last one in this sense; the first UIP is the one closest to the conflict. Cutting the graph just after the first UIP puts that node and all the earlier-level literals feeding the conflict side on the reason side of the cut. The learned clause contains the negations of the literals on the reason side that have an edge across the cut. It has exactly one literal of the conflict level, the negated UIP, plus literals of earlier levels. That single conflict-level literal is what makes the clause asserting: after undoing the conflict level, every other literal is false and the UIP's negation is forced.

## Resolving back to the first UIP

The UIP is found without drawing the graph. Start with the falsified clause. While it contains more than one literal of the conflict level, take the one whose variable was assigned most recently and resolve the clause with that variable's reason clause. Example at level 2: decide $x_3 = 1$; $x_5 = 1$ by $(\neg x_3 \vee x_5)$; $x_6 = 0$ by $(\neg x_5 \vee \neg x_6)$; $x_7 = 1$ by $(\neg x_5 \vee x_7)$; and the clause $(x_6 \vee \neg x_7 \vee \neg x_1)$ is falsified, with $x_1 = 1$ from level 1. Two level-2 literals, $x_6$ and $x_7$; the later is $x_7$, so resolve with its reason: $(x_6 \vee \neg x_1 \vee \neg x_5)$. Still two level-2 literals; resolve on $x_6$ with $(\neg x_5 \vee \neg x_6)$: $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_5)$. Only $\neg x_5$ remains at level 2, so $x_5$ is the first UIP and $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_5)$ is learned.

## Why the first UIP

Other cuts are just as sound. Resolving one more step in the example, on $x_5$ with $(\neg x_3 \vee x_5)$, gives the last-UIP clause $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_3)$, which here equals the all-decision clause. The falsified clause itself is also implied, but it has two conflict-level literals, so after backjumping it is not unit and asserts nothing. Experiments comparing learning schemes found first UIP consistently best: it stops as early as possible, so the clause tends to be short and to mention implied literals that summarize many decisions, and the learned clauses generalize to more of the search space. The resolution count is bounded by the number of literals at the conflict level, so analysis is linear in the trail. Solvers then shrink the clause further by clause minimization, which removes literals implied by others already in it.

## Going deeper

label: Non-chronological backtracking
lesson:
# Non-chronological backtracking

After learning a clause, a CDCL solver does not simply undo its last decision. It jumps back to the level at which the learned clause first becomes unit, often many levels earlier, discarding decisions that had nothing to do with the conflict. This non-chronological backtracking, or backjumping, is what lets CDCL escape regions of the search that DPLL would grind through. Computing the backjump level from a learned clause is quick, and it is an exact rule.

## The second-highest level

A first-UIP clause has exactly one literal at the conflict level $c$ and its other literals at lower levels. The solver backjumps to the highest of those lower levels, the second-highest level appearing in the clause. There, every literal except the UIP literal is still false and the UIP literal is unassigned, so the clause is unit and propagation asserts it immediately. Example: a conflict at level 4 learns a clause whose literals sit at levels 4, 1 and 2. The backjump level is 2: levels 3 and 4 are undone, and the clause forces its level-4 literal's negation at level 2. If the learned clause has a single literal, it is a unit clause true regardless of any decision, so the solver backjumps to level 0 and the literal becomes a permanent fact.

## From trail to backjump level

In practice the clause comes from conflict analysis, so the two steps chain: compute the first-UIP clause from the trail, then read off its levels. In the first-UIP example, the trail at level 2 produced $(\neg x_1 \vee \neg x_5)$, where $x_1$ was set at level 1 and $x_5$ at level 2. The second-highest level is 1, so the solver undoes level 2 and, at level 1, propagates $x_5 = 0$ from the learned clause. That propagation may cascade into further implications at level 1 or even an immediate new conflict, which is analyzed the same way. Note what happened to the decision $x_3 = 1$: it is gone, and the solver will choose its next decision afresh with the new clause in place, instead of mechanically trying $x_3 = 0$ as DPLL would.

## How much search is skipped

Chronological backtracking would return to level $c - 1$ and flip that decision. Backjumping to level $b$ undoes $c - b$ levels instead, so it skips $(c - 1) - b$ levels that chronological backtracking would have kept. A conflict at level 6 whose learned clause has literals at levels 6, 2 and 1 backjumps to level 2, skipping levels 5, 4 and 3: three levels whose decisions were irrelevant to this conflict. Those decisions may be remade later, and phase saving (re-using each variable's last value) makes the re-descent cheap when they were fine. Some solvers, on very long trails, use chronological backtracking selectively to avoid repeating expensive propagation, but the learned clause and the asserting level are computed the same way.

## Going deeper

Marques-Silva and Sakallah, "GRASP" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1999); Nadel and Ryvchin, "Chronological Backtracking" (SAT 2018).

label: Two watched literals
lesson:
# Two watched literals

Unit propagation dominates SAT run time, and the naive implementation rescans every clause that contains a newly falsified literal. The two-watched-literal scheme, introduced with the Chaff solver, watches only two literals per clause and does no work at all on backtracking. It is why modern solvers propagate millions of literals per second, and it is a model for any incremental engine that must react to local changes cheaply.

## Two watches per clause

A clause can become unit or conflicting only when all but at most one of its literals are false. So it is enough to watch two of its non-false literals: as long as both watched literals are non-false, the clause cannot be unit and need not be looked at. The solver keeps, for each literal, a watch list of the clauses watching it. When literal $\ell$ becomes false, the solver visits only the clauses on $\ell$'s watch list, not every clause containing $\ell$. Assigning $x_3 = 0$ falsifies the literal $x_3$, so the visited clauses are those watching $x_3$; clauses that contain $x_3$ but watch two other literals are untouched. To count visits from a watch table, list the clauses whose watch pair includes the falsified literal.

## Moving a watch

When a watched literal becomes false, the solver looks for a replacement: a literal of the clause that is not false and is not the other watch. If one exists, the watch moves there and the clause leaves this watch list. If none exists, the clause is unit (the other watch is unassigned and must be set true) or conflicting (the other watch is false too), and the watch stays. In this course the scan goes from the start of the clause. Example: $(x_1 \vee \neg x_2 \vee x_3 \vee x_4)$ watches $x_1$ and $\neg x_2$. When $x_1$ becomes false, the scan skips $x_1$ (false) and $\neg x_2$ (the other watch) and moves the watch to $x_3$: one move. When $x_4$ becomes false nothing happens, since it is not watched. When $x_3$ becomes false, no replacement remains, so the clause is unit and forces $\neg x_2$: no move. Total: 1 move.

## Why it beats occurrence lists

An occurrence-list solver visits every clause that contains the falsified literal; the watched scheme visits only the clauses watching it. If $\neg x_3$ occurs in 40 clauses but is watched in 6, assigning $x_3 = 1$ costs 6 visits instead of 40, and long clauses benefit most because only 2 of their literals are ever watched. The second advantage is backtracking: unassigning literals can only make watched literals non-false again, which never breaks the invariant, so the watch lists need no update when the solver backjumps. Counter-based schemes had to restore a counter per clause on every undo. Implementations also keep a blocking literal next to each watch-list entry, so a clause already satisfied by that literal is skipped without touching its memory, which matters for cache behaviour.

## Going deeper

Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang and Malik, "Chaff: Engineering an Efficient SAT Solver" (DAC 2001); Een and Sorensson, "An Extensible SAT-solver" (SAT 2003).

label: The VSIDS decision heuristic
lesson:
# The VSIDS decision heuristic

Which variable a CDCL solver decides next matters as much as how it learns. VSIDS (variable state independent decaying sum) answers with a score per variable that is bumped whenever the variable takes part in a conflict and decays over time, so the search focuses on the variables of recent conflicts. It is cheap, needs no look-ahead, and with small variations it is the default heuristic in most industrial and open-source solvers.

## Bumping with a growing increment

Each variable has an activity, initially 0. On each conflict, every variable in the learned clause is bumped: its activity grows by the current increment. Then the increment is divided by a decay factor $d < 1$, so later bumps count more than earlier ones. With $d = 0.5$ the increments are 1, 2, 4, 8, ... Suppose three conflicts learn clauses over $\{x_1, x_2\}$, then $\{x_2, x_3\}$, then $\{x_2\}$. The increments are 1, 2 and 4, so $x_1$ ends at 1, $x_3$ at 2, and $x_2$ at $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$. With $d = 0.8$ the increments are 1, 1.25, 1.5625, ..., a gentler bias toward the present. Real solvers use decay factors between about 0.8 and 0.95, and rescale all activities when the increment grows too large for floating point.

## Picking the next decision

At each decision the solver picks the unassigned variable with the highest activity. Assigned variables are skipped, however active, because they already have values. In the example above, with $x_2$ assigned, the candidates are $x_1$ (activity 1) and $x_3$ (activity 2), so the solver decides on $x_3$. The value is usually taken from phase saving, the variable's most recent value, rather than from the score. To make this fast, solvers keep unassigned variables in a binary heap ordered by activity: bumping a variable is a heap update, finding the best is constant time, and variables re-enter the heap when backjumping unassigns them. The effect is that after a conflict the solver tends to branch on the variables involved in it, which keeps the search local to the part of the formula currently causing trouble.

## Explicit decay gives the same ranking

The original formulation decays explicitly: on each conflict, multiply every activity by $d$, then add 1 to each learned-clause variable. On the same three conflicts with $d = 0.5$: after the first, $x_1 = x_2 = 1$. After the second, decay to 0.5 and 0.5, then bump $x_2$ and $x_3$: $x_1 = 0.5$, $x_2 = 1.5$, $x_3 = 1$. After the third, decay to 0.25, 0.75 and 0.5, then bump $x_2$: $x_2 = 1.75$. These are exactly the growing-increment scores (1, 7, 2) multiplied by $d^2 = 0.25$, and in general by $d^{k-1}$ after $k$ conflicts. Because all scores are scaled by the same factor, the ranking is identical. The growing increment is preferred because it touches only the bumped variables instead of every variable on every conflict.

## Going deeper

label: Restarts and the Luby sequence
lesson:
# Restarts and the Luby sequence

A CDCL solver restarts by clearing its trail back to decision level 0 while keeping everything it has learned. Restarts protect it against early bad decisions that would otherwise trap it in a hard part of the search. When to restart is a policy question, and the classic answers are the Luby sequence and geometric schedules. They are simple enough to compute by hand and important enough that every solver exposes them as a tunable parameter.

## The Luby sequence

The Luby sequence is 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, ... It is defined by $t_i = 2^{k-1}$ if $i = 2^k - 1$, and otherwise $t_i = t_{i - 2^{k-1} + 1}$ for $2^{k-1} \le i < 2^k - 1$. In words: the first $2^k - 1$ terms are two copies of the first $2^{k-1} - 1$ terms followed by $2^{k-1}$. So term 7 is 4, terms 8 to 14 repeat terms 1 to 7, and term 15 is 8. To find term 12, note $8 \le 12 < 15$, so $t_{12} = t_{12 - 8 + 1} = t_5 = 1$. Luby, Sinclair and Zuckerman showed that this schedule is within a logarithmic factor of the best possible restart strategy for any randomized algorithm whose run-time distribution is unknown, which is why it became a default. Each term is a power of two, and the sum of the first $2^k - 1$ terms is $k \cdot 2^{k-1}$, so the total work grows only slightly faster than the number of runs.

## Restart budgets

A solver multiplies the Luby sequence by a unit $u$: run $j$ lasts $u \cdot t_j$ conflicts, and then the solver restarts. The total number of conflicts by the end of run $r$ is $u \sum_{j=1}^{r} t_j$. With $u = 100$ and $r = 6$, the terms are 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, summing to 8, so 800 conflicts have been performed. The sequence keeps returning to short runs while occasionally allowing long ones: by term 15 a run of 8 units occurs, and the longest run grows without bound. That combination is what a restart policy needs: frequent restarts to escape bad early decisions, plus ever longer runs so that hard instances that need long uninterrupted search can still be finished.

## Geometric schedules and what survives a restart

A geometric schedule starts with $c$ conflicts and multiplies by a factor $g > 1$: run $j$ lasts $\lfloor c \cdot g^{j-1} \rfloor$ conflicts. With $c = 100$ and $g = 1.5$, the first three runs last 100, 150 and 225 conflicts, 475 in total. Geometric schedules restart less and less often, the opposite of Luby's recurring short runs. Whatever the schedule, a restart clears only the trail: learned clauses stay, VSIDS activities stay, and saved phases stay, so the solver usually re-descends quickly into a similar region and then diverges where the new clauses and scores say it should. Modern solvers often replace fixed schedules by dynamic ones that restart when recent learned clauses look worse (higher LBD) than the long-run average.

## Going deeper

Luby, Sinclair and Zuckerman, "Optimal Speedup of Las Vegas Algorithms" (Information Processing Letters, 1993); Huang, "The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning" (IJCAI 2007); Audemard and Simon, "Refining Restarts Strategies for SAT and UNSAT" (CP 2012).

label: Preprocessing: variable elimination and subsumption
lesson:
# Preprocessing: variable elimination and subsumption

Before search, and sometimes between restarts, a SAT solver rewrites the formula into an equisatisfiable one that is smaller or easier. Bounded variable elimination and subsumption are the two workhorses. CNF produced by Tseitin encoding of circuits is full of variables that can be eliminated cheaply, so preprocessing can remove a large share of the formula before the search even starts.

## Eliminating a variable by resolution

Let $P$ be the clauses containing $x$ and $N$ the clauses containing $\neg x$. Replacing $P \cup N$ by all resolvents of a clause of $P$ with a clause of $N$ on $x$ gives a formula without $x$ that is satisfiable exactly when the original is (Davis-Putnam elimination). Resolvents that contain some literal and its negation are tautologies and are dropped. Example: $P = \{(x \vee a), (x \vee b \vee \neg c)\}$ and $N = \{(\neg x \vee \neg a), (\neg x \vee c)\}$. The four pairs resolve to $(a \vee \neg a)$, a tautology; $(a \vee c)$; $(b \vee \neg c \vee \neg a)$; and $(b \vee \neg c \vee c)$, a tautology. So elimination produces 2 non-tautological resolvents. A model of the new formula extends to $x$: set $x$ so that every clause of $P$ and $N$ is satisfied, which the resolvents guarantee is possible.

## When elimination pays

Eliminating $x$ can multiply clauses: $|P| \cdot |N|$ resolvents replace $|P| + |N|$ clauses. Bounded variable elimination, as in the SatELite preprocessor, eliminates $x$ only if the count does not grow. In the example, 2 resolvents replace $2 + 2 = 4$ clauses, a net change of $2 - 4 = -2$, so $x$ is eliminated. With $|P| = |N| = 3$ and no tautologies, 9 resolvents would replace 6 clauses, a net change of $+3$, and $x$ would stay. Tseitin variables of gates with few fan-outs often pass the test, which is why circuit-derived CNF shrinks so much. The solver records the eliminated clauses so that, after finding a model of the reduced formula, it can reconstruct values for the eliminated variables in reverse order.

## Subsumption

Clause $C$ subsumes clause $D$ if every literal of $C$ is in $D$. Then $D$ is implied by $C$ and can be deleted without changing the set of models. Among $(a \vee b)$, $(a \vee b \vee \neg c)$, $(\neg a \vee c)$ and $(b)$, the clause $(b)$ subsumes both $(a \vee b)$ and $(a \vee b \vee \neg c)$, and $(a \vee b)$ also subsumes $(a \vee b \vee \neg c)$, so two clauses can go; count each deletable clause once even when several clauses subsume it. Subsumption checks use occurrence lists and signatures (bit masks of the variables) to avoid comparing every pair. A related rule, self-subsuming resolution, shortens a clause: from $(a \vee b)$ and $(\neg a \vee b \vee c)$ the resolvent $(b \vee c)$ subsumes the second clause, which can be replaced by it.

## Going deeper

Een and Biere, "Effective Preprocessing in SAT through Variable and Clause Elimination" (SAT 2005); Biere et al. (eds.), "Handbook of Satisfiability" (2nd ed., 2021), the chapter on preprocessing.

label: BDD reduction rules
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# BDD reduction rules

A binary decision diagram starts life as a decision tree: test one variable per level, branch on its value, and read 0 or 1 at the leaves. Two reduction rules turn the tree into a compact, canonical graph: merge isomorphic subgraphs and delete tests whose two outcomes are the same. Knowing exactly what each rule removes is how a tool designer reasons about BDD size, memory and the cost of building BDDs for real logic.

## From decision tree to diagram

Fix a variable order, say $x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_n$. The complete decision tree tests $x_1$ at the root, $x_2$ at both children, and so on, so level $i$ holds $2^i$ nodes for $i = 0, \dots, n - 1$ and the bottom holds $2^n$ leaves, one per assignment, each labelled with the function's value. The number of nonterminal (decision) nodes is $1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1$. For $n = 3$ that is 7 decision nodes and 8 leaves; for $n = 20$ it is over a million nodes, no matter how simple the function is. A tree is just a truth table drawn as a graph, so it is useless for large functions; all the compression comes from the reductions that follow. In this course node counts always mean nonterminal nodes, with the two terminals 0 and 1 not counted.

## Merging isomorphic subgraphs

The first rule merges any two nodes that test the same variable and have the same children, bottom-up; all leaves with the same value merge into one terminal. Applied alone, it gives the quasi-reduced BDD, in which every path still tests every variable. Its level $i$ has one node per distinct cofactor of $f$ by the first $i$ variables of the order. Take $f = (x_1 \wedge x_2) \vee x_3$ with order $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$. Level 0 has $f$ itself. Level 1 has the cofactors $f|_{x_1=0} = x_3$ and $f|_{x_1=1} = x_2 \vee x_3$: 2 nodes. Level 2 has the cofactors by $x_1$ and $x_2$: $x_3$, $x_3$, $x_3$ and 1, which are 2 distinct functions: 2 nodes. The quasi-reduced BDD has $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ nonterminal nodes, against 7 in the tree.

## Removing redundant tests

The second rule deletes a node whose low and high children are the same node, redirecting its parents to that child: the test does not matter. In the quasi-reduced BDD of $(x_1 \wedge x_2) \vee x_3$, the level-1 node for $x_3$ tests $x_2$ but both its children are the $x_3$ node, and the level-2 node for the constant 1 tests $x_3$ with both children equal to the terminal 1. Both are removed, leaving 3 nodes, one per variable: the reduced ordered BDD (ROBDD). Applying both rules until neither applies gives a unique result for each function and order, which is Bryant's canonicity theorem: two functions are equal exactly when their ROBDDs are the same graph. So the redundant-test rule removed $5 - 3 = 2$ nodes. Packages never build the tree or the quasi-reduced form; they apply both rules on the fly through a unique table, so every node is created already reduced.

## Going deeper

Bryant, "Graph-Based Algorithms for Boolean Function Manipulation" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1986); Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", volume 4A, section 7.1.4.

label: Reduced ordered BDDs
lesson:
# Reduced ordered BDDs

A reduced ordered BDD represents a Boolean function canonically for a fixed variable order: equal functions give identical graphs, so equivalence is a pointer comparison. That property made BDDs the first practical engine for equivalence checking and symbolic model checking, and they remain the workhorse wherever many operations are done on the same functions. Counting ROBDD nodes for small functions is how you build the intuition for which functions are cheap and which are not.

## Counting nodes from a formula

The ROBDD has one node for each distinct subfunction that arises by cofactoring along the order and that actually depends on the variable being tested. To count, cofactor the function variable by variable in the order, collect the distinct non-constant results, and assign each to the first variable of the order it depends on. Take $f = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus x_3$ with order $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$. Testing $x_1$ needs 1 node. Its cofactors are $x_2 \oplus x_3$ and its complement, 2 distinct functions, each depending on $x_2$: 2 nodes. Their cofactors by $x_2$ are $x_3$ and $\neg x_3$: 2 nodes. Total 5. For $f = (x_1 \vee x_2) \wedge x_3$, the cofactors by $x_1$ are $x_2 \wedge x_3$ and $x_3$; the first needs an $x_2$ node whose high child is the same $x_3$ node, so the total is 3.

## Counting nodes from a truth table

When a function is given by its on-set, the list of inputs where it is 1, split the list by the first variable of the order, then by the next, and compare the pieces. Let $f$ be 1 exactly on $x_1x_2x_3 \in \{000, 011, 101, 110\}$ with order $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$. Splitting by $x_1$: for $x_1 = 0$ the remaining on-set over $x_2x_3$ is $\{00, 11\}$, which is XNOR; for $x_1 = 1$ it is $\{01, 10\}$, which is XOR. They differ, so the root needs 2 children, each a node on $x_2$. Splitting each by $x_2$ gives $x_3$ or $\neg x_3$, and both pieces share those two $x_3$ nodes. Total $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$; the function is even parity, which needs 5 nodes in every order. When a split produces two equal pieces, the test is redundant and that node does not exist.

## Shared BDDs and canonicity

A BDD package stores all functions in one shared graph with a unique table that maps (variable, low, high) to an existing node. Building a node first looks it up, so any subfunction that occurs twice, in one function or in two, is stored once. Store $f = x_1 \wedge x_2$ and $g = x_2$ with order $x_1 < x_2$. The ROBDD of $f$ is an $x_1$ node whose high child is the $x_2$ node; that $x_2$ node is exactly the ROBDD of $g$. The shared graph holds 2 nodes, not $2 + 1 = 3$. Canonicity makes equivalence free: after building two circuits' outputs, they are equivalent exactly when their roots are the same node. Packages such as CUDD also use complemented edges, so a function and its negation share one graph; with them, node counts differ from the plain counts used in this course.

## Going deeper

Bryant, "Graph-Based Algorithms for Boolean Function Manipulation" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1986); Somenzi, the CUDD package documentation; Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", volume 4A, section 7.1.4.

label: BDD variable ordering
lesson:
# BDD variable ordering

The same function can have a BDD with a handful of nodes under one variable order and an exponential number under another. Choosing the order is therefore the main lever a BDD-based tool has, and it is a hard optimization problem. The classic example, a sum of products of variable pairs, shows the gap exactly and explains the rule of thumb that related variables belong close together in the order.

## A function that rewards interleaving

Let $f = x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 + \dots + x_n y_n$. Under the interleaved order $x_1 < y_1 < x_2 < y_2 < \dots$, the BDD tests $x_1$; if it is 0, the first product is false and the path moves on to the next pair; if it is 1, it tests $y_1$, which either makes $f$ true or moves on to the next pair. At every point the graph only needs to remember which pair it is on, so each pair contributes one $x_i$ node and one $y_i$ node: $2n$ nonterminal nodes in total. For $n = 3$ that is 6 nodes, and for $n = 100$ it is 200. The width of every level is 1. Information flows through the order locally, which is the property good orders have in common.

## The same function under a bad order

Under the separated order $x_1 < \dots < x_n < y_1 < \dots < y_n$, the BDD must read all the $x$ variables before any $y$. When it reaches $y_1$, the remaining function is $\bigvee_{i \in S} y_i$, where $S$ is the set of indices with $x_i = 1$, and different sets give different functions. So the $x$ levels form a complete tree: level $i$ needs $2^i$ nodes, $2^n - 1$ in all. The $y$ levels need one node for each distinct function $\bigvee_{i \in S'} y_i$ with $S'$ nonempty, organized so that level $y_j$ holds $2^{n-j}$ nodes, another $2^n - 1$. The total is $2^{n+1} - 2$: 14 for $n = 3$, against 6 interleaved, and over $2 \cdot 10^{30}$ for $n = 100$. The function did not change; only the amount of state the order forces the diagram to carry did.

## Comparing orders and finding good ones

For a general function, compare orders by building the ROBDD under each and counting nodes, and expect differences in both directions. Finding an optimal order is NP-hard, and even improving a given order is NP-complete, so packages use heuristics. Static heuristics order variables from the circuit structure, for example by a depth-first traversal from the outputs so that inputs feeding the same gates sit together. Dynamic reordering by sifting, due to Rudell, moves one variable at a time through every position, keeps the best, and repeats; swapping two adjacent levels is a local operation, which makes sifting affordable. Reordering is triggered when the node count grows past a threshold. A tool designer should remember that some functions, such as the middle bits of a multiplier, have exponential BDDs under every order, so no reordering can save them.

## Going deeper

label: The ite and apply operations
prereqs: Logical connectives: AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES
lesson:
# The ite and apply operations

Every operation a BDD package offers, from AND and XOR to existential quantification, is built on one recursive procedure: split both arguments on the top variable, recurse on the cofactors, and rebuild through the unique table. The if-then-else operator ite packages this into a single primitive. Knowing how apply recurses, and why a computed table bounds its cost, is how you predict the run time of symbolic algorithms such as image computation.

## ite as the universal operator

Define $\text{ite}(f, g, h) = f g + \neg f h$: if $f$ then $g$ else $h$. Every binary connective is an ite with constant or negated arguments: $f \wedge g = \text{ite}(f, g, 0)$, $f \vee g = \text{ite}(f, 1, g)$, $f \oplus g = \text{ite}(f, \neg g, g)$ and $\neg f = \text{ite}(f, 0, 1)$. A BDD node testing $x$ with children $L$ and $H$ is itself $\text{ite}(x, H, L)$, so the package needs only one core algorithm. Its result is always the canonical ROBDD of the combined function, so its size can be predicted by building that function directly. Take $f = x_1 \wedge x_2$ and $g = x_3$ under $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$. Then $f \vee g$ has a root on $x_1$ whose low child is the $x_3$ node and whose high child is an $x_2$ node with children $x_3$ and 1: 3 nonterminal nodes.

## Apply for XOR

Apply computes $u \text{ op } v$ recursively. If both arguments are terminals, return the terminal for the operation's value. Otherwise let $x$ be the earliest variable in the order at the top of $u$ or $v$, take the cofactors of each argument with respect to $x$ (an argument that does not test $x$ is its own cofactor), recurse on the two pairs, and return the unique node $(x, \text{low}, \text{high})$, or the child itself if both are equal. For $f = x_1 \vee x_2$ and $g = x_2 \vee x_3$ under $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$, $f \oplus g$ is 1 exactly on 001 and 100, which is $\neg x_2 \wedge (x_1 \oplus x_3)$. Its ROBDD has a root on $x_1$, two $x_2$ nodes (one leading to $x_3$, one to $\neg x_3$) and two $x_3$ nodes: 5 nonterminal nodes. XOR rarely simplifies at terminals, which is why it tends to cost more than AND or OR.

## The computed table and the product bound

Without memoization apply would revisit the same pair of nodes many times along different paths and could take exponential time. The computed table caches the result of each call keyed by (op, $u$, $v$), so each pair of nodes is processed at most once. Every call's arguments are one node of $F$ and one node of $G$, so the number of distinct calls is at most $|F| \cdot |G|$, with sizes counting terminals: for 19 and 12 nodes, at most 228 calls. The result can also be as large as the product, as with some XORs. Three-argument ite is bounded by $|F| \cdot |G| \cdot |H|$. Real packages make the computed table a lossy hash cache rather than a complete memo, trading occasional recomputation for bounded memory; the bound is still the right model for planning.

## Going deeper

Brace, Rudell and Bryant, "Efficient Implementation of a BDD Package" (DAC 1990); Bryant, "Graph-Based Algorithms for Boolean Function Manipulation" (1986).

label: Counting satisfying assignments on a BDD
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Counting satisfying assignments on a BDD

Once a function is a BDD, counting its satisfying assignments takes one pass over the graph, even when the count is astronomically large. The same pass gives signal probabilities, uniform sampling of solutions and the weights used in probabilistic analysis. The only subtlety is that a reduced BDD skips levels, and every skipped variable doubles the number of assignments a path stands for.

## Counting paths to 1

Number the levels of the order $0, \dots, n - 1$ and give both terminals level $n$. Process nodes bottom-up. For the terminals, the count is 1 for terminal 1 and 0 for terminal 0. For a node $u$ at level $\ell(u)$ with children $L$ and $H$, $\text{count}(u) = \text{count}(L) \cdot 2^{\ell(L) - \ell(u) - 1} + \text{count}(H) \cdot 2^{\ell(H) - \ell(u) - 1}$, which counts assignments to the variables from $u$'s level downward. The total is $\text{count}(\text{root}) \cdot 2^{\ell(\text{root})}$. Example over $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$: the root tests $x_1$ with low child the terminal 1 and high child a node testing $x_3$ (low 0, high 1). The $x_3$ node, at level 2, has count $0 + 1 = 1$. The root, at level 0, has count $1 \cdot 2^{3-0-1} + 1 \cdot 2^{2-0-1} = 4 + 2 = 6$. The function is $\neg x_1 \vee x_3$, true on 6 of 8 inputs.

## Skipped levels

Skipped levels are where hand counts go wrong. An edge from level $\ell(u)$ to a child at level $\ell(c)$ skips $\ell(c) - \ell(u) - 1$ variables, each free, so it multiplies the child's count by $2^{\ell(c) - \ell(u) - 1}$. Take order $x_1 < x_2 < x_3 < x_4$, root testing $x_1$ with low child a node $a$ testing $x_4$ (low 0, high 1) and high child a node $b$ testing $x_2$ (low 0, high 1). Node $a$ is at level 3: count 1. Node $b$ is at level 1, and its high edge to the terminal skips $x_3$ and $x_4$: count $1 \cdot 2^{4-1-1} = 4$. The root's low edge to $a$ skips $x_2$ and $x_3$: $1 \cdot 2^{3-0-1} = 4$; its high edge to $b$ skips nothing: $4 \cdot 1 = 4$. Total 8, and indeed $\neg x_1 x_4 + x_1 x_2$ is true on 4 + 4 inputs. Work is linear in the number of nodes.

## From counts to probabilities

Dividing the count by $2^n$ gives the probability that a uniformly random input satisfies $f$: for $\neg x_1 \vee x_3$, $6/8 = 0.75$. If each input $x_i$ is 1 with its own probability $p_i$, the same bottom-up pass computes $P(u) = (1 - p_i) P(L) + p_i P(H)$ for a node testing $x_i$, with $P = 1$ and $P = 0$ at the terminals and skipped variables contributing a factor of 1. That is the signal probability that power estimators and random-pattern testability tools need. Counting also enables uniform sampling: walk down from the root and take each child with probability proportional to its weighted count, which picks every satisfying assignment with equal probability. Constrained-random stimulus generators in verification use BDD-based sampling of this kind for small constraint sets, and switch to SAT- or SMT-based samplers when BDDs grow too large.

## Going deeper

Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", volume 4A, section 7.1.4; Bryant, "Graph-Based Algorithms for Boolean Function Manipulation" (1986).

label: Why multipliers blow up BDDs
lesson:
# Why multipliers blow up BDDs

BDDs made combinational equivalence checking routine for control logic and adders, and then hit a wall on multipliers. The wall is not a tuning problem: Bryant proved that some output bits of integer multiplication have exponential BDDs under every variable order. Understanding that result tells a tool designer when to stop trying to reorder and switch to SAT sweeping, word-level methods or algebraic reasoning instead.

## Bryant's lower bound for multiplication

For an $n$-bit by $n$-bit multiplier, Bryant showed in 1991 that the ROBDD of the middle output bit, bit $n - 1$, has size exponential in $n$ under every variable order; the bound he proved grows like $2^{n/8}$. The argument is a communication argument: whatever the order, there is a level at which the variables above and below must exchange many bits of information to determine the middle bit, and each distinct piece of information is a distinct subfunction at that level, so a distinct node. Low output bits are easy (bit 0 is a single AND) and the highest bits are easier than the middle ones; the middle bits collect the most partial products and carries. The practical meaning is blunt: building BDDs for the outputs of a 32-bit or 64-bit multiplier is hopeless, and dynamic reordering cannot help, because no good order exists.

## Adders versus multipliers

Adders show what good structure looks like. Under the interleaved order $a_0 < b_0 < a_1 < b_1 < \dots$, each sum bit's BDD only has to carry the current carry from one bit position to the next, so the size is linear in $n$. Under the separated order with all $a$ bits first, the diagram must remember all of $a$ before it sees $b$, and the size becomes exponential. So adders are easy only with the right order, while multipliers are hard with every order. The difference is locality: in addition, information flows from bit $i$ to bit $i + 1$ through one carry; in multiplication every output bit mixes products $a_i b_j$ from across both operands, so no order keeps the interacting bits close. Comparators and multiplexers behave like adders; dividers and the middle bits of multipliers do not.

## What verification tools do instead

Equivalence of two similar multiplier netlists, such as before and after local synthesis, is proved by SAT sweeping: the netlists share many internal equivalent nodes, which are proved bottom-up so that each SAT call stays small. For architecturally different multipliers (Booth versus array, for example), few internal equivalences exist, and the effective methods are word-level or algebraic: computer-algebra approaches model each gate as a polynomial and rewrite the specification polynomial, such as $\sum 2^i z_i - (\sum 2^i a_i)(\sum 2^j b_j)$, backwards through the gates until it reduces to zero. Earlier, Bryant and Chen's multiplicative binary moment diagrams (*BMDs) represented word-level multiplication compactly by changing the decomposition, not the order. In model checking, datapath multipliers are usually abstracted as uninterpreted functions so that BDDs or SAT only reason about the control logic around them.

## Going deeper

Bryant, "On the Complexity of VLSI Implementations and Graph Representations of Boolean Functions with Application to Integer Multiplication" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1991); Bryant and Chen, "Verification of Arithmetic Circuits with Binary Moment Diagrams" (DAC 1995).

problems.e: Reading the bit pairs together lets the BDD carry only the current carry between levels, so each bit adds a constant number of nodes.

An adder is built with all a bits ordered before all b bits. What happens to its BDD?

A) It shrinks, because the a bits can be shared

B) It stays linear, as adders are always easy

C) It becomes identical to the multiplier BDD

D) It grows exponentially, because the BDD must remember all of a before seeing b
problems.a: It grows exponentially, because the BDD must remember all of a before seeing b
problems.e: The same function can be linear or exponential depending on the order; adders are only easy under orders that pair related bits.

problems.q:
Multiplicative binary moment diagrams (*BMDs) were proposed for arithmetic. What do they change compared with BDDs?

A) They use a better variable order for the same Boolean BDD

B) They only represent adders

C) They drop canonicity to save memory

D) They represent word-level functions with moments and edge weights, so integer multiplication has a compact form
problems.a: They represent word-level functions with moments and edge weights, so integer multiplication has a compact form
problems.e: *BMDs decompose by linear moments with multiplicative weights; the word-level product becomes small even though its bit-level BDDs are exponential.

problems.q:
Two multiplier netlists differ only by local synthesis optimizations. Which method usually proves them equivalent?

A) Exhaustive simulation of all inputs

B) Building the full output BDDs

C) SAT-based equivalence checking that exploits the many internal equivalent nodes

D) Random simulation alone
problems.a: SAT-based equivalence checking that exploits the many internal equivalent nodes
problems.e: Structural similarity gives many internal equivalences; SAT sweeping proves them step by step, so each SAT call stays small.

problems.q:
A model checker uses BDDs for the control logic of a DSP block containing a multiplier. What is a common way to keep it tractable?

A) Order the multiplier inputs first

B) Abstract the multiplier as an uninterpreted function or cut it out, and verify it separately

C) Disable garbage collection

D) Increase the BDD cache size
problems.a: Abstract the multiplier as an uninterpreted function or cut it out, and verify it separately
problems.e: Control properties rarely depend on the exact product, so abstracting the datapath avoids the provable blow-up.

label: Miters for equivalence checking
lesson:
# Miters for equivalence checking

Equivalence checking asks whether two circuits compute the same outputs for every input, for example RTL against its synthesized netlist. The miter turns that universal question into a single satisfiability question: build a circuit that outputs 1 exactly when the two designs disagree, and ask a SAT solver whether it can ever output 1. Every combinational equivalence checker, from ABC's cec to commercial signoff tools, is organized around this construction.

## Building the miter

Feed the same primary inputs to both circuits $A$ and $B$, XOR each pair of corresponding outputs, and OR the XORs into a single miter output. The miter is 1 on an input vector exactly when some output differs there, so the circuits are equivalent if and only if the miter output is unsatisfiable. A satisfying assignment is a distinguishing vector, the counterexample. For small circuits the miter can be evaluated by truth table. Let $A = x_1 \wedge x_2$ and $B = x_1 \wedge (x_2 \vee x_3)$. They agree whenever $x_1 = 0$, and when $x_1 = 1$ they differ only if $x_2 = 0$ and $x_3 = 1$. So exactly 1 of the 8 input vectors, 101, drives the miter to 1, and that vector is what a checker would report. Counting distinguishing vectors is the same as counting the 1s of $A \oplus B$.

## Sizing the miter glue

With the Tseitin convention from the SAT subdomain, the glue on top of the two circuits costs, for $n \ge 2$ output pairs: $n$ XOR gates at 4 clauses each, one $n$-input OR at $n + 1$ clauses, and one unit clause asserting that the miter output is 1. That is $4n + (n + 1) + 1 = 5n + 2$ clauses and $n + 1$ new variables (one per XOR, one for the OR). For 4 output pairs the glue adds 22 clauses and 5 variables. The glue is tiny next to the circuits themselves, which is why the miter costs essentially nothing to build. What makes a miter hard is not its size but the lack of shared structure between $A$ and $B$, which forces the solver to discover their equivalence from scratch.

## Sharing inputs and structure

Because both circuits read the same inputs, the primary inputs appear once in the miter CNF. The total variable count is therefore the shared inputs, plus the gates of $A$, plus the gates of $B$, plus the glue: for 10 inputs, 50 gates in $A$, 60 in $B$ and 2 outputs, $10 + 50 + 60 + (2 + 1) = 123$ variables. In practice checkers do not hand this raw CNF to the solver. They first merge the two circuits into one and-inverter graph with structural hashing, so identical logic in $A$ and $B$ becomes one node, and then prove internal equivalences bottom-up. When most outputs land on the same node after hashing, the remaining SAT problems are small. A miter per output cone, rather than one global miter, also keeps each query focused and reports exactly which output differs.

## Going deeper

Brand, "Verification of Large Synthesized Designs" (ICCAD 1993); Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton and Een, "Improvements to Combinational Equivalence Checking" (ICCAD 2006); the ABC documentation for cec.

problems.q: Circuit A computes (x1 ∨ x3) ∧ x2 and circuit B computes (x1 ∨ x3) ⊕ x2 over the inputs $x_1, x_2, x_3$. Their miter XORs the two outputs. On how many of the 8 input vectors is the miter output 1?
problems.e: The miter is 1 exactly where the circuits disagree. Comparing the two truth tables, they differ on 7 input vectors.

problems.q: Circuit A computes (x2 ∧ x3) ⊕ ¬x1 and circuit B computes ¬x1 ∧ x3 over the inputs $x_1, x_2, x_3$. Their miter XORs the two outputs. On how many of the 8 input vectors is the miter output 1?
problems.e: The miter is 1 exactly where the circuits disagree. Comparing the two truth tables, they differ on 4 input vectors.

problems.q: Circuit A computes (¬x2 ⊕ ¬x1) ∧ ¬x3 and circuit B computes x2 ∧ x3 over the inputs $x_1, x_2, x_3$. Their miter XORs the two outputs. On how many of the 8 input vectors is the miter output 1?
problems.e: The miter is 1 exactly where the circuits disagree. Comparing the two truth tables, they differ on 4 input vectors.

problems.q: Two circuits with 2 outputs each are joined into a miter: one XOR per output pair and one 2-input OR of the XORs. With one Tseitin variable per gate, how many new variables does the miter glue add?
problems.e: One variable per XOR (2) plus one for the OR: 3.

problems.q: Two circuits with 8 outputs each are joined into a miter: one XOR per output pair and one 8-input OR of the XORs, whose output is asserted to be 1. Using Tseitin encoding (2-input XOR: 4 clauses; k-input OR: k + 1 clauses; one unit clause for the assertion), how many clauses does the miter glue add on top of the two circuits?
problems.e: XORs: 4·8 = 32. OR: 8 + 1 = 9. Assertion: 1. Total 42.

problems.e: One variable per XOR (3) plus one for the OR: 4.

The miter shares the inputs, XORs each output pair and ORs the XORs. With one Tseitin variable per primary input and per gate, how many variables does the whole miter CNF have?
problems.e: Inputs are shared, so they count once: 11 + 72 + 22 + (2 XORs + 1 OR) = 108.

The miter shares the inputs, XORs each output pair and ORs the XORs. With one Tseitin variable per primary input and per gate, how many variables does the whole miter CNF have?
problems.e: Inputs are shared, so they count once: 12 + 12 + 68 + (6 XORs + 1 OR) = 99.

The miter shares the inputs, XORs each output pair and ORs the XORs. With one Tseitin variable per primary input and per gate, how many variables does the whole miter CNF have?
problems.e: Inputs are shared, so they count once: 22 + 16 + 105 + (2 XORs + 1 OR) = 146.

label: Structural hashing of AIGs
lesson:
# Structural hashing of AIGs

And-inverter graphs (AIGs) represent logic with only two-input AND nodes and inverted edges. Structural hashing keeps them free of duplicate nodes: before creating an AND node, look up its pair of inputs in a hash table and reuse an existing node if there is one. It is the cheapest simplification in equivalence checking and synthesis, and in ABC it is the first thing done to any network, through the strash command.

## Hashing AND nodes

Each AIG node is $n = \text{AND}(p, q)$, where $p$ and $q$ are literals: a primary input or node, possibly complemented. Structural hashing normalizes the pair, for example by sorting the two literals, and uses it as a key. If the key is in the table, the new node is not created: its readers use the existing node. Otherwise a node is created and its key inserted. Take $n_1 = \text{AND}(a, b)$, $n_2 = \text{AND}(b, a)$, $n_3 = \text{AND}(n_1, \neg c)$ and $n_4 = \text{AND}(a, b)$. The key $\{a, b\}$ is created by $n_1$; $n_2$ and $n_4$ hit it and merge into $n_1$. Two AND nodes remain, $n_1$ and $n_3$. Complemented literals are different keys: $\text{AND}(a, \neg b)$ does not merge with $\text{AND}(a, b)$.

## Cascading merges

Hashing runs in topological order, and a merge can enable later merges. When a node is merged, every reader is redirected to its representative before the reader's own key is computed. Continue the example with $n_5 = \text{AND}(n_2, \neg c)$. Since $n_2$ was merged into $n_1$, the key of $n_5$ is $\{n_1, \neg c\}$, which is exactly the key of $n_3$, so $n_5$ merges too. A single pass in topological order catches every such cascade, because each node's inputs are final by the time it is processed. Count the result by walking the list in order, replacing inputs by their representatives, and adding a node only when its normalized key is new. Two circuits that are copies of each other up to input order of the gates collapse completely into one graph this way.

## Trivial simplifications

Hashing is usually combined with one-level rewriting rules applied before the lookup: $\text{AND}(x, x) = x$, $\text{AND}(x, \neg x) = 0$, $\text{AND}(x, 1) = x$ and $\text{AND}(x, 0) = 0$. A node removed this way becomes an alias for a literal or a constant, and its readers see that literal, which can trigger further simplifications and merges downstream. Take $n_1 = \text{AND}(a, b)$, $n_2 = \text{AND}(n_1, n_1)$, $n_3 = \text{AND}(n_2, \neg n_1)$ and $n_4 = \text{AND}(c, n_2)$. Then $n_2$ becomes $n_1$, $n_3$ becomes $\text{AND}(n_1, \neg n_1) = 0$, and $n_4$ becomes $\text{AND}(c, n_1)$, a new key: 2 AND nodes remain. Structural hashing only finds structural identity. Two nodes computing the same function with different structure, such as $\text{AND}(a, \text{AND}(b, c))$ and $\text{AND}(\text{AND}(a, b), c)$, stay distinct; finding those needs simulation and SAT sweeping.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann, Paruthi, Krohm and Ganai, "Robust Boolean Reasoning for Equivalence Checking and Functional Property Verification" (IEEE TCAD, 2002); Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-Aware AIG Rewriting" (DAC 2006); the ABC documentation for strash.

problems.q: An AIG over inputs a, b, c, d has, in topological order: n1 = AND(¬b, d); n2 = AND(¬n1, ¬b); n3 = AND(¬b, n2); n4 = AND(d, ¬b); n5 = AND(¬b, d). Structural hashing keys each node by its pair of input literals, in either order, after replacing already-merged inputs by their representatives. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?
problems.e: Walking the nodes in order and looking each normalized input pair up in the hash table, 2 of the 5 nodes are merged or simplified away, leaving 3.

problems.q: An AIG over inputs a, b, c, d has, in topological order: n1 = AND(¬a, ¬b); n2 = AND(d, a); n3 = AND(a, ¬n1); n4 = AND(¬b, ¬n2); n5 = AND(¬n2, ¬b); n6 = AND(¬a, ¬b); n7 = AND(a, d); n8 = AND(¬n2, ¬b). Structural hashing keys each node by its pair of input literals, in either order, after replacing already-merged inputs by their representatives. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?
problems.e: Walking the nodes in order and looking each normalized input pair up in the hash table, 4 of the 8 nodes are merged or simplified away, leaving 4.

Structural hashing keys each node by its pair of input literals, in either order, after replacing already-merged inputs by their representatives. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?
problems.e: Walking the nodes in order and looking each normalized input pair up in the hash table, 2 of the 5 nodes are merged or simplified away, leaving 3.

Structural hashing keys each node by its pair of input literals, in either order, after replacing already-merged inputs by their representatives. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?
problems.e: Walking the nodes in order and looking each normalized input pair up in the hash table, 3 of the 6 nodes are merged or simplified away, leaving 3.

Structural hashing keys each node by its pair of input literals, in either order, after replacing already-merged inputs by their representatives. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?

Structural hashing keys each node by its pair of input literals, in either order, after replacing already-merged inputs by their representatives. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?
problems.e: Walking the nodes in order and looking each normalized input pair up in the hash table, 5 of the 9 nodes are merged or simplified away, leaving 4.

Before hashing it also applies AND(x, x) = x and AND(x, ¬x) = 0. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?

Before hashing it also applies AND(x, x) = x and AND(x, ¬x) = 0. How many AND nodes remain after one pass in this order?
problems.e: Walking the nodes in order and looking each normalized input pair up in the hash table, 5 of the 10 nodes are merged or simplified away, leaving 5.

label: Combinational equivalence checking
lesson:
# Combinational equivalence checking

Combinational equivalence checking (CEC) proves that two netlists with matching state elements compute the same next-state and output functions. It runs after every synthesis, optimization and ECO step in a production flow, so it must be fast, fully automatic and trustworthy. Its engine is a pipeline: match the designs, build miters, simplify aggressively, and leave as little as possible for the SAT solver.

## The CEC flow

CEC needs a correspondence between the two designs: primary inputs and outputs by name, and registers matched one to one, usually by name and then by structural or functional matching for renamed ones. With registers matched, each register's output becomes a shared free input (a pseudo-input) and its next-state function a pseudo-output, so the sequential designs reduce to a set of combinational comparisons, one per output or register input. Each comparison is a miter over that output's cone of logic. A satisfiable miter gives a distinguishing vector over inputs and register values; an unsatisfiable one proves that cone equivalent. If synthesis retimed or re-encoded the registers so that no one-to-one correspondence exists, the problem is no longer combinational and needs sequential equivalence checking.

## Simplify before you solve

Modern CEC engines are organized so that the SAT solver sees as little as possible. First, both designs are merged into one AIG with structural hashing, which proves structurally identical logic equivalent for free; when synthesis made only local changes, many outputs already meet at the same node. Second, random simulation computes a signature for every node; nodes with different signatures are certainly different. Third, SAT sweeping proves candidate internal equivalences bottom-up and merges each proved pair, often with cut points, so that later queries are small. Counterexamples to internal candidates are not design bugs; they are added to the simulation patterns to split other wrong candidates. Only after this does the engine solve the output miters, which are by then usually trivial. Synthesized netlists have many internal equivalences with their source because synthesis mostly makes local changes, which is what makes this pipeline work.

## Engines and results

BDDs and SAT both decide CEC. BDDs are canonical, so once both outputs are built, comparison is free, but building them fails on large datapaths and multipliers. SAT with sweeping scales to large netlists and is the default today. In ABC the command cec runs the full simulation, sweeping and SAT pipeline; Yosys offers equivalence passes (the equiv family) that check designs it has transformed itself. A result must be read carefully. UNSAT on every miter is a proof. A counterexample may still reflect an under-specified environment: if it drives an input combination the system never applies, the designs may be equivalent under a missing constraint, and the fix is an assumption, not an RTL change. A timeout on one cone is not a proof, though the other cones remain proved.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann et al., "Robust Boolean Reasoning for Equivalence Checking and Functional Property Verification" (IEEE TCAD, 2002); Mishchenko et al., "Improvements to Combinational Equivalence Checking" (ICCAD 2006).

problems.q:
The miter for output z is satisfiable. What does the satisfying assignment represent?

A) An input vector (and register state) on which the two designs produce different values of z

B) A proof that z is equivalent

C) The set of gates that differ

D) A list of internal equivalences
problems.a: An input vector (and register state) on which the two designs produce different values of z
problems.e: The miter output is 1 exactly when the circuits disagree, so a model is a distinguishing vector, the counterexample.

problems.q:
A synthesis run renamed and retimed registers so that no one-to-one register correspondence exists. Can plain combinational equivalence checking prove the result?

A) Only if the design has no outputs

B) Yes, after structural hashing

C) Yes, by matching registers by name

D) No: without register correspondence the check becomes sequential
problems.a: No: without register correspondence the check becomes sequential
problems.e: Retiming moves state across logic, so combinational cones no longer line up and a sequential method is needed.

problems.q:
The miter for output z is satisfiable. What does the satisfying assignment represent?

A) A proof that z is equivalent

B) An input vector (and register state) on which the two designs produce different values of z

C) A list of internal equivalences

D) The set of gates that differ
problems.a: An input vector (and register state) on which the two designs produce different values of z
problems.e: The miter output is 1 exactly when the circuits disagree, so a model is a distinguishing vector, the counterexample.

problems.q:
A SAT call disproves a candidate equivalence between internal nodes. What does a good CEC engine do with the counterexample?

A) Discard it and continue

B) Add it to the simulation patterns to split other wrong candidate classes

C) Delete both nodes

D) Report the designs as non-equivalent
problems.a: Add it to the simulation patterns to split other wrong candidate classes
problems.e: An internal non-equivalence is not a design bug, but the vector often refines several other candidate classes at once.

problems.q:
Why does a CEC engine run random simulation before calling the SAT solver?

A) SAT solvers require a simulation trace as input

B) Simulation proves the remaining equivalences

C) Cheap simulation separates most non-equivalent node pairs, leaving only likely equivalences for SAT

D) Simulation computes the variable order
problems.a: Cheap simulation separates most non-equivalent node pairs, leaving only likely equivalences for SAT
problems.e: Two nodes with different simulation signatures are certainly different; only nodes with equal signatures need a SAT proof.

problems.q:
After structural hashing of both netlists into one AIG, the two outputs land on the same node. What does that mean?

A) The hash table collided and the check must restart

B) They are proved equivalent with no SAT call

C) They are equivalent only for random inputs

D) The circuits are different
problems.a: They are proved equivalent with no SAT call
problems.e: Structural hashing merges identical AND structure; if both outputs map to one node they compute the same function.

problems.q:
The equivalence checker reports a counterexample in which an input is driven to a value the real system never applies. What is the right reading?

A) The designs differ only outside the legal input space, so a constraint (assumption) on that input is missing

B) The checker has a bug

C) The simulation patterns were too short

D) The designs are equivalent
problems.a: The designs differ only outside the legal input space, so a constraint (assumption) on that input is missing
problems.e: Combinational checks consider all input combinations; designs optimized with don't-care inputs need those constraints stated explicitly.

problems.q:
When are BDDs a better choice than SAT for a combinational equivalence check?

A) When the designs have no structural similarity and many inputs

B) When the cones have small BDDs under a good order, such as control logic

C) When the cone contains a large multiplier

D) Always, because BDDs are canonical
problems.a: When the cones have small BDDs under a good order, such as control logic
problems.e: Canonical BDDs compare in constant time once built, but building them only works when the functions have small BDDs.

problems.q:
In ABC, which command performs combinational equivalence checking of two networks?

A) pdr

B) bmc3

C) cec

D) strash only
problems.a: cec
problems.e: cec builds the miter and runs the simulation, sweeping and SAT engine; pdr and bmc3 are sequential property checkers.

label: SAT sweeping and simulation signatures
lesson:
# SAT sweeping and simulation signatures

SAT sweeping, also called fraiging in ABC, finds and merges functionally equivalent nodes inside one AIG. It combines cheap random simulation, which rules out most false candidates, with SAT calls that prove the rest. In equivalence checking it collapses two similar designs into one graph from the inputs upward; in synthesis it removes redundancy. Its cost model, simulation classes and one SAT call per candidate, is easy to compute and drives engine tuning.

## Simulation signatures

Apply $k$ random input vectors (in practice as 64-bit words, so 64 vectors per pass) and record each node's output on each vector: its $k$-bit signature. If two nodes have different signatures, some vector distinguishes them, so they are certainly not equivalent. If their signatures are equal, they are candidates. Grouping nodes by signature gives candidate equivalence classes; a class with one member needs no further work. With signatures $n_1$: 1010, $n_2$: 0110, $n_3$: 1010, $n_4$: 0110, $n_5$: 1111, there are two candidate classes, $\{n_1, n_3\}$ and $\{n_2, n_4\}$, and $n_5$ is a singleton. More vectors split more false classes; the right number is a trade-off between simulation time and wasted SAT calls on candidates that fail.

## Proving candidates with SAT

For each class, pick a representative, typically the node closest to the inputs, and prove every other member equal to it with one SAT call on a small miter of the two nodes. A class of size $s$ costs $s - 1$ calls if every candidate holds; in the example, $1 + 1 = 2$ calls. Sweeping proceeds in topological order, and each proved pair is merged immediately, so that later queries see the merged graph and stay small; proved nodes can also be treated as cut points. A failing call returns a counterexample vector, which is not a bug in the design: it is added to the simulation patterns and re-run, which typically splits several other wrong classes at once. Engines also limit the conflicts per call and skip candidates that are too hard, since an unproved candidate only costs optimization, not soundness.

## Equivalence up to complement

Logic often contains a node and the complement of another, for example after De Morgan rewriting, and AIGs represent inverters on edges for free. So sweepers treat $u$ and $\neg v$ as candidates too: a signature and its bitwise complement belong in the same class. The usual trick is to normalize each signature, say by complementing it when its first (or last) bit is 1, and then group the normalized signatures. With $n_1$: 1100, $n_2$: 0011, $n_3$: 1100 and $n_4$: 1010, normalizing so the first bit is 0 maps $n_1$ and $n_3$ to 0011, the same as $n_2$, so $\{n_1, n_2, n_3\}$ is one class with mixed phases and $n_4$ is alone. Each proof then checks either $u = v$ or $u = \neg v$ according to the phases, and the merge connects readers through an inverted edge.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Jiang and Brayton, "FRAIGs: A Unifying Representation for Logic Synthesis and Verification" (ERL technical report, 2005); Kuehlmann et al., "Robust Boolean Reasoning for Equivalence Checking and Functional Property Verification" (IEEE TCAD, 2002).

problems.q: After 8 rounds of random simulation the AIG nodes have signatures n1: 01101111, n2: 01101111, n3: 01111101, n4: 10111110, n5: 10110110, n6: 10110110, n7: 10111110, n8: 01111101. Nodes with identical signatures are candidate equivalences. How many candidate classes contain at least two nodes?
