label: Cube generalization in IC3
lesson:
# Cube generalization in IC3

The clause IC3 learns when it blocks a state is only as useful as the number of states it excludes. Generalization shrinks the blocked cube literal by literal, keeping each step relatively inductive, so that one clause rules out a large region of the state space. It is where IC3 spends most of its time and where engine implementations differ most, so it is a natural place for a tool designer to tune.

## Why generalize

A blocked state $s$ assigns every latch, so the clause $\neg s$ excludes a single state out of $2^n$. Blocking states one at a time would make IC3 an explicit-state search, hopeless on designs with hundreds of latches. Generalization looks for a sub-cube $c \subseteq s$, with fewer literals, that can be blocked in its place; removing a literal doubles the number of states the clause excludes. A generalized clause must keep the two properties that made $\neg s$ usable: initiation (the cube $c$ contains no initial state) and relative inductiveness ($F_{i-1} \wedge \neg c \wedge T \rightarrow \neg c'$). Generalization never affects soundness, only performance: IC3 with no generalization is still correct, just extremely slow. In practice the reasons a state is unreachable involve a few related latches, so short clauses usually exist.

## Dropping a literal

To test whether a literal can be dropped from cube $s$, form the smaller cube $c$ and run both checks: $c$ must contain no initial state, and no state of the frame $F$ outside $c$ may have a transition into $c$. Example with states $x_2x_1x_0$, initial state 000, $F = \{000, 001, 010\}$, transitions 000 → 001, 001 → 010, 010 → 000 and 010 → 100, and blocked cube $x_2 \wedge x_1 \wedge \neg x_0$ (the state 110). Dropping the $x_2$ literal gives $x_1 \wedge \neg x_0 = \{010, 110\}$; the state 001 of $F$ steps to 010, so it fails. Dropping $x_1$ gives $x_2 \wedge \neg x_0 = \{100, 110\}$; 010 steps to 100, so it fails. Dropping $x_0$ gives $x_2 \wedge x_1 = \{110, 111\}$; no state of $F$ steps into it and it avoids 000, so it passes: the clause $\neg(x_2 \wedge x_1)$ can be learned.

## MIC and unsat cores

Engines generalize in stages. First, the UNSAT proof of the relative-inductiveness query for $\neg s$ often uses only some literals of $s'$; literals whose assumptions are absent from the unsat core can be dropped at once, for free. Then the down or MIC procedure (minimal inductive clause) tries to drop each remaining literal in turn, re-checking with one SAT call per attempt, and keeps a literal only when dropping it breaks the check. Stronger variants handle counterexamples to generalization: when a drop fails because of a predecessor state, ctgDown-style generalization tries to block that predecessor at an earlier frame and then retries the drop. Each refinement buys shorter clauses at the cost of more queries, so the generalization strategy is a policy choice, a trade-off between effort per clause and the number of clauses and frames IC3 needs.

## Going deeper

Bradley, "SAT-Based Model Checking without Unrolling" (VMCAI 2011); Hassan, Bradley and Somenzi, "Better Generalization in IC3" (FMCAD 2013).

problems.q:
A generalized clause mentions only 3 of 200 latches. Why is that often enough?

A) The reason a state is unreachable usually involves a few related latches

B) Short clauses are always inductive

C) IC3 only reads 3 latches

D) The other latches are constants
problems.a: The reason a state is unreachable usually involves a few related latches
problems.e: Real invariants tend to be local, such as a one-hot or counter-range fact about a few registers.

problems.q:
What does dropping a literal from a blocked cube do to the set of states the clause excludes?

A) Leaves it unchanged

B) Doubles it, because the dropped variable may now take either value

C) Makes it empty

D) Halves it
problems.a: Doubles it, because the dropped variable may now take either value
problems.e: A cube with one literal fewer covers twice as many states, so its negation excludes twice as many.

problems.q:
A generalized clause mentions only 3 of 200 latches. Why is that often enough?

A) The reason a state is unreachable usually involves a few related latches

B) IC3 only reads 3 latches

C) Short clauses are always inductive

D) The other latches are constants
problems.a: The reason a state is unreachable usually involves a few related latches
problems.e: Real invariants tend to be local, such as a one-hot or counter-range fact about a few registers.

problems.q:
States are bit vectors x2x1x0. Transitions: 000 → 010; 001 → 000, 101; 010 → 001, 111; 011 → 010, 111; 100 → 011, 110; 101 → 110, 111; 110 → 110; 111 → 110. The initial state is 000 and the frame is $F =$ {000, 011, 100, 110}. IC3 blocks the cube ¬x2 ∧ ¬x1 ∧ x0 (the state 001), which is inductive relative to $F$. Generalization tries to drop one literal: the smaller cube must still contain no initial state, and no state of $F$ outside it may step into it. Which choice is correct?

A) No single literal can be dropped

B) Drop the literal on x2

C) Drop the literal on x0

D) Drop the literal on x1
problems.a: Drop the literal on x2
problems.e: Dropping a literal doubles the cube. Only the cube that avoids 000 and receives no transition from the rest of F survives the check.

problems.q:
States are bit vectors x2x1x0. Transitions: 000 → 001, 101; 001 → 010; 010 → 101; 011 → 100; 100 → 111; 101 → 010; 110 → 010, 111; 111 → 111. The initial state is 000 and the frame is $F =$ {000, 011, 100, 101, 111}. IC3 blocks the cube x2 ∧ x1 ∧ ¬x0 (the state 110), which is inductive relative to $F$. Generalization tries to drop one literal: the smaller cube must still contain no initial state, and no state of $F$ outside it may step into it. Which choice is correct?

A) Drop the literal on x1

B) No single literal can be dropped

C) Drop the literal on x0

D) Drop the literal on x2
problems.a: No single literal can be dropped
problems.e: Each 2-literal cube either contains 000 or receives a transition from a state of F outside it, so the full cube must be blocked as it is.

problems.q:
States are bit vectors x2x1x0. Transitions: 000 → 111; 001 → 100, 110; 010 → 011; 011 → 101; 100 → 110; 101 → 101; 110 → 101, 111; 111 → 001. The initial state is 000 and the frame is $F =$ {000, 001, 100}. IC3 blocks the cube x2 ∧ ¬x1 ∧ x0 (the state 101), which is inductive relative to $F$. Generalization tries to drop one literal: the smaller cube must still contain no initial state, and no state of $F$ outside it may step into it. Which choice is correct?

A) Drop the literal on x0

B) Drop the literal on x1

C) Drop the literal on x2

D) No single literal can be dropped
problems.a: Drop the literal on x2
problems.e: Dropping a literal doubles the cube. Only the cube that avoids 000 and receives no transition from the rest of F survives the check.

problems.q:
The down/MIC procedure tries to drop each literal of a cube in turn. What does it do when dropping a literal breaks relative inductiveness?

A) Drops two literals instead

B) Keeps that literal and moves on to the next one

C) Restarts with the original cube

D) Reports a counterexample
problems.a: Keeps that literal and moves on to the next one
problems.e: MIC searches for a minimal inductive subclause by greedily trying to drop literals and keeping the ones that are necessary.

problems.q:
The down/MIC procedure tries to drop each literal of a cube in turn. What does it do when dropping a literal breaks relative inductiveness?

A) Keeps that literal and moves on to the next one

B) Reports a counterexample

C) Restarts with the original cube

D) Drops two literals instead
problems.a: Keeps that literal and moves on to the next one
problems.e: MIC searches for a minimal inductive subclause by greedily trying to drop literals and keeping the ones that are necessary.

problems.q:
A relative-inductiveness query for ¬c is UNSAT. How can the solver's unsat core shrink c for free?

A) The core lists clauses to delete from F

B) The core forces all literals to stay

C) Literals of c' whose assumptions are not in the core can be dropped

D) The core gives a counterexample to the query
problems.a: Literals of c' whose assumptions are not in the core can be dropped
problems.e: If the proof did not use a literal of the primed cube, the query is still UNSAT without it.

label: Abstraction refinement (CEGAR)
lesson:
# Abstraction refinement (CEGAR)

Counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) proves properties of a design by model checking a smaller abstract model and refining it only where a spurious counterexample shows it is too coarse. Localization abstraction, which frees latches the property does not seem to need, is its most common form in hardware. The loop is a template that reappears in cut-point equivalence checking, in IC3 variants and in software model checkers.

## The CEGAR loop

CEGAR repeats four steps. Abstract: build a model that over-approximates the design, so that every concrete behavior has an abstract counterpart. Check: model check the property on the abstraction. If it holds, it holds on the design, because no concrete path can reach a bad state when no abstract path can; stop. If it fails, concretize: try to follow the abstract counterexample on the real design, typically with a BMC query constrained to the abstract trace. If the concrete trace exists, it is a real bug; stop. Otherwise the counterexample is spurious: refine the abstraction so that it no longer allows this trace, and repeat. On a finite design the loop terminates, because each refinement adds precision and the worst case is the concrete design itself.

## Existential abstraction

Hiding variables gives an existential abstraction. Each concrete state maps to the abstract state that keeps only the visible variables; an abstract state is initial if some concrete initial state maps to it; and there is an abstract transition from $a$ to $b$ whenever some concrete transition goes from a state mapping to $a$ to one mapping to $b$, whether or not that concrete source is reachable. Example: states $x_2x_1x_0$, hide $x_0$, so abstract states are $x_2x_1$. Concrete transitions 000 → 001, 001 → 010, 010 → 010, 011 → 110 and 110 → 110, initial state 000. Concretely, 000, 001 and 010 are reachable, projecting to 00 and 01. Abstractly, 00 → 00 and 00 → 01, and from 01 the edge 011 → 110 gives 01 → 11, although 011 is unreachable. So 3 abstract states are reachable, one more than the projection.

## Spurious counterexamples and refinement

Extra abstract states and edges are where spurious counterexamples come from. In localization abstraction, a hidden latch becomes a free input that can change arbitrarily each cycle, so an abstract trace may need it to jump from 0 to 1 with no cause. Refinement makes the responsible latches concrete again. Proof-based refinement runs BMC on the concrete design along the counterexample's length; when it is UNSAT, the unsat core names the latches and constraints the infeasibility depends on, and exactly those are added back. Predicate abstraction, common in software model checking, tracks the truth of chosen predicates such as $x < y$ and refines by adding predicates, often obtained by Craig interpolation. Over-approximation is essential: an abstraction that drops behaviors could miss bugs, so it could never prove safety. Abstraction pays off when the property depends on a small part of a large design.

## Going deeper

Clarke, Grumberg, Jha, Lu and Veith, "Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement" (CAV 2000); McMillan and Amla, "Automatic Abstraction without Counterexamples" (TACAS 2003).

problems.q:
In counterexample-guided abstraction refinement, what does the model checker run on first?

A) An abstract model that over-approximates the design's behavior

B) A random simulation trace

C) The full concrete design

D) An under-approximation with fewer behaviors
problems.a: An abstract model that over-approximates the design's behavior
problems.e: The abstraction is smaller, and because it includes every concrete behavior, a proof on it carries over to the design.

problems.q:
Which order of steps describes one CEGAR iteration?

A) Model check, abstract, refine, concretize

B) Abstract, model check, concretize the counterexample, refine if it is spurious

C) Concretize, abstract, prove, refine

D) Refine, abstract, simulate, report
problems.a: Abstract, model check, concretize the counterexample, refine if it is spurious
problems.e: Refinement happens only when a counterexample cannot be realized on the concrete system.

problems.q:
The abstract model satisfies the safety property. What can be concluded about the design?

A) The design fails it

B) Nothing: the abstraction may hide bugs

C) The design satisfies it too

D) Only that BMC must be run next
problems.a: The design satisfies it too
problems.e: Every concrete path maps to an abstract path, so no concrete path can reach a bad state if no abstract path can.

problems.q:
A concrete system has states x2x1x0 with transitions 000 → 010; 001 → 100, 101; 010 → 000; 011 → 111; 100 → 110, 111; 101 → 101; 110 → 000; 111 → 001 and initial state 000. Localization abstraction hides x0: an abstract state is the pair x2x1, and there is an abstract transition whenever some concrete transition maps onto it. How many abstract states are reachable from 00?

A) 1

B) 5

C) 2

D) 4
problems.e: The abstraction has an edge for every concrete edge, whether or not its source is reachable, so it reaches 4 abstract states, while the reachable concrete states project onto only 2. The extra ones are where spurious counterexamples come from.

problems.q:
A concrete system has states x2x1x0 with transitions 000 → 010; 001 → 110; 010 → 011; 011 → 111; 100 → 111; 101 → 110; 110 → 000; 111 → 101 and initial state 000. Localization abstraction hides x0: an abstract state is the pair x2x1, and there is an abstract transition whenever some concrete transition maps onto it. How many abstract states are reachable from 00?

A) 4

B) 1

C) 2

D) 6
problems.e: The abstraction has an edge for every concrete edge, whether or not its source is reachable, so it reaches 4 abstract states, while the reachable concrete states project onto only 4. The extra ones are where spurious counterexamples come from.

problems.q:
A concrete system has states x2x1x0 with transitions 000 → 001; 001 → 100; 010 → 001, 010; 011 → 011, 100; 100 → 000, 010; 101 → 110; 110 → 101, 111; 111 → 000, 110 and initial state 000. Localization abstraction hides x0: an abstract state is the pair x2x1, and there is an abstract transition whenever some concrete transition maps onto it. How many abstract states are reachable from 00?

A) 3

B) 2

C) 4

D) 1
problems.e: The abstraction has an edge for every concrete edge, whether or not its source is reachable, so it reaches 4 abstract states, while the reachable concrete states project onto only 3. The extra ones are where spurious counterexamples come from.

problems.q:
Localization abstraction makes some latches free inputs. An abstract counterexample needs a hidden latch to jump from 0 to 1 with no cause. What kind of counterexample is it?

A) Spurious: the real latch cannot change that way

B) Incomplete: BMC must go deeper

C) Real: the abstraction is exact

D) Vacuous: the property is trivially true
problems.a: Spurious: the real latch cannot change that way
problems.e: Freed latches can take any value each cycle, which the real logic may forbid.

problems.q:
A BMC check of the concrete design along the abstract counterexample's length is UNSAT. What does the UNSAT proof tell the refinement?

A) Which latches or constraints the infeasibility depends on, through the unsat core

B) The real counterexample

C) Which inputs are unused

D) That the abstraction is too precise
problems.a: Which latches or constraints the infeasibility depends on, through the unsat core
problems.e: Proof-based refinement adds the latches mentioned in the core, which are enough to rule out that counterexample.

problems.q:
Predicate abstraction tracks the truth of chosen predicates such as x < y instead of the variables. How does it refine?

A) It ignores the counterexample

B) It adds new predicates, often found by interpolation from the spurious counterexample

C) It makes all variables concrete at once

D) It removes predicates
problems.a: It adds new predicates, often found by interpolation from the spurious counterexample
problems.e: New predicates distinguish the abstract states that the spurious path merged.

label: SMT over bit-vectors
lesson:
# SMT over bit-vectors

Hardware is made of fixed-width words, and the SMT theory of bit-vectors models them exactly: arithmetic wraps modulo $2^n$, shifts drop bits, and signed and unsigned operations are distinct. Word-level model checkers, equivalence checkers and symbolic simulators send their queries to bit-vector solvers, which mostly answer by bit-blasting to SAT. Evaluating bit-vector terms precisely and estimating their bit-blasted size are both everyday skills for a formal tool designer.

## Bit-vector terms and wraparound

In SMT-LIB, a bit-vector of width $n$ is a string of $n$ bits, and most operations act on the unsigned value modulo $2^n$. With 4-bit $a = 1101$ (13) and $b = 0110$ (6): bvadd gives $19 \bmod 16 = 3$; bvsub gives 7; bvmul gives $78 \bmod 16 = 14$. Shifts take a bit-vector shift amount: bvshl $a$ by 2 gives $0100 = 4$, since the top bits fall off; bvlshr $a$ by 1 gives $0110 = 6$, filling with 0; bvashr $a$ by 1 copies the sign bit and gives $1110 = 14$, the signed value -2. The extract operation ((_ extract 3 2) a) keeps bits 3 down to 2, $11 = 3$, and concat joins bit-vectors. Because all of this is exact, a bit-vector model captures overflow bugs that integer arithmetic would hide.

## Bit-blasting cost

Bit-blasting translates each operation into a gate-level circuit and then into CNF with the Tseitin encoding. A ripple-carry adder for $n$-bit bvadd uses a half adder at bit 0 (one XOR and one AND, $4 + 3 = 7$ clauses and 2 gate variables) and full adders at bits 1 to $n - 1$ (two XORs, two ANDs and one OR, $8 + 6 + 3 = 17$ clauses and 5 gate variables each). Clauses: $7 + 17(n - 1)$; for $n = 8$, $7 + 119 = 126$. Variables, counting the $2n$ operand bits: $2n + 2 + 5(n - 1)$; for $n = 8$, $16 + 2 + 35 = 53$. Addition is linear in width, but an $n$-bit multiplier is quadratic, which is why solvers simplify at the word level (constant multiplications, shifts, extracts of known bits) before bit-blasting, and why wide multipliers stay hard for SAT.

## Signed interpretation

The same bits have an unsigned and a signed (two's complement) reading. In $n$ bits the top bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$, so an 8-bit pattern ranges over -128 to 127 when signed. Arithmetic is identical for both readings; only the interpretation differs. Example: 8-bit $100 + 50 = 150$, the pattern 10010110, which reads as $150 - 256 = -106$ when signed: signed overflow, though the unsigned sum is fine. Comparisons are where the readings really diverge: bvult and bvslt give different answers for 10010110 against 00000001 (150 is not below 1 unsigned, but -106 is below 1 signed). Division and remainder also come in unsigned and signed versions, and right shifts in logical and arithmetic versions. Many RTL bugs are a signed comparison written as unsigned, and a bit-vector solver will find them exactly.

## Going deeper

Kroening and Strichman, "Decision Procedures" (2nd ed., 2016), chapter 6; the SMT-LIB standard, the FixedSizeBitVectors theory.

problems.q: In SMT-LIB, a and b are 8-bit vectors with a = #b01000010 (66) and b = #b01011011 (91). What is the value of ((_ extract 7 5) a), read as an unsigned integer?
problems.e: Bit-vector arithmetic wraps modulo $2^{8} = 256$; shifts drop bits off the end (bvashr copies the sign bit in); extract keeps the named bits. The result is 2.

problems.q: In SMT-LIB, a and b are 4-bit vectors with a = #b0101 (5) and b = #b1111 (15). What is the value of (bvmul a b), read as an unsigned integer?
problems.e: Bit-vector arithmetic wraps modulo $2^{4} = 16$; shifts drop bits off the end (bvashr copies the sign bit in); extract keeps the named bits. The result is 11.

problems.q: In SMT-LIB, a and b are 8-bit vectors with a = #b11110010 (242) and b = #b01011001 (89). What is the value of (bvxor a b), read as an unsigned integer?
problems.e: Bit-vector arithmetic wraps modulo $2^{8} = 256$; shifts drop bits off the end (bvashr copies the sign bit in); extract keeps the named bits. The result is 171.

problems.q: A solver bit-blasts a 8-bit bvadd as a ripple-carry adder: a half adder at bit 0 (one XOR, one AND) and full adders elsewhere (two XOR, two AND, one OR). Counting one variable per input bit of both operands and one per gate, how many variables does it use?
problems.e: Inputs: 2·8 = 16. Gates: 2 + 5·7 = 37. Total 53.

problems.q: A solver bit-blasts a 5-bit bvadd as a ripple-carry adder: a half adder at bit 0 (one XOR, one AND) and full adders elsewhere (two XOR, two AND, one OR). Counting one variable per input bit of both operands and one per gate, how many variables does it use?
problems.e: Inputs: 2·5 = 10. Gates: 2 + 5·4 = 22. Total 32.

problems.q: A solver bit-blasts a 20-bit bvadd as a ripple-carry adder: a half adder at bit 0 (one XOR, one AND) and full adders elsewhere (two XOR, two AND, one OR). Counting one variable per input bit of both operands and one per gate, how many variables does it use?
problems.e: Inputs: 2·20 = 40. Gates: 2 + 5·19 = 97. Total 137.

problems.q: a and b are 4-bit vectors with a = #b1111 and b = #b1010. What is the value of (bvsub a b) read as a two's-complement signed integer?
problems.e: The 4-bit result pattern is 0101. Reading the top bit with weight $-2^{3}$ gives the signed value 5 (unsigned 5).

problems.q: a and b are 8-bit vectors with a = #b00000100 and b = #b00000101. What is the value of (bvmul a b) read as a two's-complement signed integer?
problems.e: The 8-bit result pattern is 00010100. Reading the top bit with weight $-2^{7}$ gives the signed value 20 (unsigned 20).

problems.q: a and b are 8-bit vectors with a = #b11111101 and b = #b11101011. What is the value of (bvmul a b) read as a two's-complement signed integer?
problems.e: The 8-bit result pattern is 00111111. Reading the top bit with weight $-2^{7}$ gives the signed value 63 (unsigned 63).

label: Uninterpreted functions and congruence closure
lesson:
# Uninterpreted functions and congruence closure

The theory of equality with uninterpreted functions (EUF) lets a solver reason about terms like f(a) without knowing what f computes: the only fact it uses is that equal arguments give equal results. In hardware verification, EUF abstracts datapath units, such as an ALU or a multiplier, so that proofs about control logic do not have to reason about arithmetic. Its decision procedure, congruence closure, is fast and incremental, which makes it a building block of every SMT solver.

## Congruence closure

Given equalities between terms, congruence closure computes all equalities they imply in EUF. It keeps equivalence classes of terms in a union-find structure. First merge the classes of each asserted equality. Then apply congruence: whenever $s$ and $t$ are in one class, merge the classes of $f(s)$ and $f(t)$; repeat until nothing changes. Example with constants $a, b, c, d$ and terms $a, b, c, d, f(a), f(b), f(c)$, assuming $a = b$ and $f(a) = c$. The asserted equalities give classes $\{a, b\}$ and $\{f(a), c\}$. Since $a$ and $b$ are equal, congruence merges $f(a)$ with $f(b)$, giving $\{c, f(a), f(b)\}$. Nothing else merges: $d$ and $f(c)$ stay alone. So the terms fall into 4 classes: $\{a, b\}$, $\{c, f(a), f(b)\}$, $\{d\}$ and $\{f(c)\}$.

## Chains of congruence

Congruence can cascade through nested applications. Assume $a = f(a)$ and consider the terms $a$, $f(a)$, $f(f(a))$ and $b$. The assertion merges $a$ with $f(a)$. Since $a$ and $f(a)$ are now in one class, congruence merges $f(a)$ with $f(f(a))$, so all three are equal; $b$ stays alone. The result is 2 classes. In general, each merge can enable congruences one level up, so the procedure keeps a list of parent terms for every class and re-examines the parents of merged classes; with this bookkeeping it runs in $O(n \log n)$ time for $n$ terms. A term is disequal to another only if a disequality was asserted; when an asserted disequality ends up inside one class, the formula is unsatisfiable, and the chain of merges that caused it is the explanation the solver reports.

## Ackermann's reduction

EUF can also be eliminated: Ackermann's reduction replaces each distinct application $f(t_i)$ by a fresh variable $v_i$ and adds the functional-consistency constraint $t_i = t_j \rightarrow v_i = v_j$ for every pair. For $m$ distinct applications that is $\binom{m}{2} = m(m-1)/2$ constraints: 10 for $m = 5$, 4950 for $m = 100$. The reduction is simple and lets a solver without EUF support decide the formula, but its quadratic growth is why solvers prefer congruence closure inside DPLL(T). In processor verification, Burch and Dill's method compares a pipelined design with its specification by abstracting the ALU and register-file contents with uninterpreted functions, so that the proof depends only on the forwarding and control logic. An uninterpreted function over-approximates the real one, so proofs carry over but counterexamples may be spurious.

## Going deeper

Nelson and Oppen, "Fast Decision Procedures Based on Congruence Closure" (Journal of the ACM, 1980); Burch and Dill, "Automatic Verification of Pipelined Microprocessor Control" (CAV 1994); Kroening and Strichman, "Decision Procedures" (2nd ed., 2016), chapter 4.

label: The theory of arrays
lesson:
# The theory of arrays

Memories, register files and FIFOs are arrays: maps from addresses to data, read and written each cycle. The SMT theory of arrays models them with two operations, select and store, and a handful of axioms. It lets a verifier reason about a memory through the addresses actually used rather than its full size, which is the only way large memories fit into a formal proof.

## Read over write

select$(a, i)$ reads array $a$ at index $i$; store$(a, i, v)$ is the array that equals $a$ except that index $i$ holds $v$. The read-over-write axiom says select(store$(a, i, v)$, $j$) is $v$ if $i = j$ and select$(a, j)$ otherwise. With concrete addresses, peel the stores from the outside in. For $b$ = store(store(store$(a, 4, 92)$, 3, 69), 2, 14): select$(b, 3)$ skips the outer store (address 2), hits the store at address 3 and returns 69. select$(b, 4)$ returns 92. select$(b, 6)$ misses all three stores and reaches the initial array: the initial content $a[6]$, which is unknown, not 0. When the same address is written twice, the later (outer) store wins, because it is peeled first.

## Symbolic addresses

With symbolic indices the comparison may be unknown, and read-over-write produces a case split. Consider select(store(store$(a, i, v)$, $j$, $w$), $k$). Compare $k$ with the outer index $j$ first: if $k = j$ is known, the result is $w$. If $k \neq j$ is known, move inward and compare $k$ with $i$: $k = i$ gives $v$, $k \neq i$ gives select$(a, k)$. If $k \neq j$ is known but nothing is known about $k$ and $i$, the result is ite$(k = i, v, \text{select}(a, k))$. If $k = i$ is known but $k$ and $j$ are unrelated, the result is ite$(k = j, w, v)$, because a matching outer store still overrides the inner one. With nothing known the term is ite$(k = j, w, \text{ite}(k = i, v, \text{select}(a, k)))$. Each ite is a case the solver must explore, so the number of stores in a chain drives the cost.

## Arrays as memories in hardware proofs

The extensionality axiom states that two arrays equal at every index are equal, which lets a solver compare whole memories. Quantifier-free formulas over select and store are decidable: read-over-write case splits on the finitely many index terms that appear reduce them to equality reasoning, so the cost depends on the accesses, not on the memory size. In BMC of a design with a memory, each cycle's write adds a store, and each read becomes a select over the chain of earlier stores; word-level SMT encodings can keep a memory as one array term instead of bit-blasting every word. A further abstraction tracks only a few addresses and returns arbitrary data for the rest. That over-approximates the memory, so proofs carry over but counterexamples can be spurious and must be checked.

## Going deeper

McCarthy, "Towards a Mathematical Science of Computation" (IFIP Congress, 1962); Bradley, Manna and Sipma, "What's Decidable About Arrays?" (VMCAI 2006); Kroening and Strichman, "Decision Procedures" (2nd ed., 2016), chapter 7.

problems.q:

A) 13

B) 94

C) 56

D) 86

E) the initial content a[2]
problems.a: the initial content a[2]
problems.e: Read-over-write peels stores from the outside in: if the store address equals the read address the stored value is the answer, otherwise the read moves to the inner array. Only when every store misses does the read reach the initial array.

B) the initial content a[5]

C) 26

D) 72
problems.e: Read-over-write peels stores from the outside in: if the store address equals the read address the stored value is the answer, otherwise the read moves to the inner array. Only when every store misses does the read reach the initial array.

problems.q:

A) 0

C) 58

D) 94

problems.a: the initial content a[7]
problems.e: Read-over-write peels stores from the outside in: if the store address equals the read address the stored value is the answer, otherwise the read moves to the inner array. Only when every store misses does the read reach the initial array.

C) ite(k = j, w, ite(k = i, v, select(a, k)))

D) ite(k = j, w, v)

problems.e: Apply read-over-write to the outer store first (compare k with j), then to the inner store (compare k with i). A known equality or disequality resolves a case; an unknown one leaves an ite that the solver must split on.

A) the value v

B) the value w

C) ite(k = j, w, ite(k = i, v, select(a, k)))

D) ite(k = i, v, select(a, k))
problems.a: ite(k = i, v, select(a, k))
problems.e: Apply read-over-write to the outer store first (compare k with j), then to the inner store (compare k with i). A known equality or disequality resolves a case; an unknown one leaves an ite that the solver must split on.

D) ite(k = j, w, ite(k = i, v, select(a, k)))

problems.e: Apply read-over-write to the outer store first (compare k with j), then to the inner store (compare k with i). A known equality or disequality resolves a case; an unknown one leaves an ite that the solver must split on.

Why is quantifier-free reasoning about arrays with read and write decidable?

A) Array formulas have no models

B) A finite number of read-over-write case splits on the index terms that appear reduces it to equality reasoning

C) Arrays are always finite in SMT

D) It reduces to linear programming
problems.a: A finite number of read-over-write case splits on the index terms that appear reduces it to equality reasoning
problems.e: Each select over a store splits on index equality, and there are finitely many index terms to compare.

problems.q:
In bounded model checking of a CPU with a register file, the register file is modelled as an array updated by store each cycle. What does a read in frame k become?

A) A select over a chain of stores from earlier frames, simplified by read-over-write

B) A constant 0

C) A bit-blasted copy of all registers

D) A fresh unconstrained value
problems.a: A select over a chain of stores from earlier frames, simplified by read-over-write
problems.e: Each write adds a store; reads look back through the chain and pick the latest write to a matching address.

problems.q:
An abstraction replaces a large memory by a small number of tracked addresses and returns arbitrary data for the rest. What kind of approximation is that?

A) An over-approximation: proofs carry over, but counterexamples may be spurious

B) An under-approximation: bugs carry over, proofs do not

C) An exact model

D) A vacuous model
problems.a: An over-approximation: proofs carry over, but counterexamples may be spurious
problems.e: Untracked reads may return values the real memory never holds, which can only add behaviors.

label: DPLL(T)
lesson:
# DPLL(T)

Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers decide formulas that mix Boolean structure with atoms from theories such as bit-vectors, arrays, uninterpreted functions and arithmetic. The dominant architecture, DPLL(T), pairs a CDCL SAT solver that handles the Boolean structure with theory solvers that check whether the chosen atoms are consistent. Understanding the split explains both SMT performance and the interfaces that hardware model checkers rely on.

## Boolean abstraction

DPLL(T) replaces each theory atom by a Boolean variable. The formula $(x < 3 \vee y = 5) \wedge x > 4$ becomes $(b_1 \vee b_2) \wedge b_3$, with $b_1$ standing for $x < 3$, $b_2$ for $y = 5$ and $b_3$ for $x > 4$. The SAT solver searches over this abstraction as usual: decide, propagate, learn. A Boolean model is only a candidate, because the abstraction forgets what the atoms mean: $b_1 = b_3 = 1$ satisfies the Boolean formula but asks for $x < 3$ and $x > 4$ at once. So every candidate, or every partial assignment in an eager-checking solver, is passed to the theory solver. When the theory solver agrees, it extends the Boolean model to concrete values, such as $x = 5$ and $y = 5$, which is the model the SMT solver returns.

## Theory checks and explanations

The theory solver checks whether the asserted literals are consistent in the theory. If not, it returns an explanation: a small subset of the literals that is already inconsistent, such as $\{x < 3, x > 4\}$. Its negation, $(\neg b_1 \vee \neg b_3)$, is a valid clause, and the SAT solver learns it exactly like a conflict clause, then backjumps. Small explanations matter, because a short clause blocks every assignment containing those literals, not just the current one. Theory solvers can also propagate: with $x = y$ and $y = z$ asserted, the EUF solver tells the SAT solver that $x = z$ must hold before it is decided, giving a reason clause, just as unit propagation does. Because the SAT solver backtracks constantly, a theory solver must also retract assertions cheaply, keeping its own trail of changes.

## Eager versus lazy and theory combination

DPLL(T) is the lazy approach: the theory is consulted during search. The eager approach translates the whole problem to SAT first, as bit-blasting does for bit-vectors. Bit-vector solvers are largely eager, after aggressive word-level rewriting, because a bit-level SAT solver is the most effective engine for fixed-width arithmetic; arithmetic over unbounded integers and EUF are handled lazily. Formulas mixing theories, such as integer arithmetic with uninterpreted functions, are solved by Nelson-Oppen combination: each theory solver works on its own atoms, and they exchange equalities between shared variables until both agree or one finds a conflict, which is complete for stably infinite theories with disjoint signatures. For hardware model checking the decisive feature is incrementality, push and pop or assumptions, since BMC and IC3 issue many small related queries.

## Going deeper

Nieuwenhuis, Oliveras and Tinelli, "Solving SAT and SAT Modulo Theories: From an Abstract Davis-Putnam-Logemann-Loveland Procedure to DPLL(T)" (Journal of the ACM, 2006); Kroening and Strichman, "Decision Procedures" (2nd ed., 2016), chapters 3 and 10.

problems.q:
An SMT solver answers SAT. What does the model contain?

A) Only truth values for the atoms

B) A list of learned clauses

C) Values for the theory variables (and functions) that satisfy the original formula

D) A proof of satisfiability
problems.a: Values for the theory variables (and functions) that satisfy the original formula
problems.e: The theory solver extends a consistent Boolean assignment to concrete theory values.

problems.q:
Why does DPLL(T) need a theory solver at all, if the SAT engine finds a Boolean model?

A) Boolean models are always theory-consistent

B) The theory solver chooses the decision order

C) A Boolean model may assign atoms truth values that no theory model can satisfy

D) The SAT engine cannot handle more than one atom
problems.a: A Boolean model may assign atoms truth values that no theory model can satisfy
problems.e: The Boolean abstraction forgets the meaning of atoms, so their combination must be checked in the theory.

problems.q:
An SMT solver answers SAT. What does the model contain?

A) Only truth values for the atoms

B) Values for the theory variables (and functions) that satisfy the original formula

C) A proof of satisfiability

D) A list of learned clauses
problems.a: Values for the theory variables (and functions) that satisfy the original formula
problems.e: The theory solver extends a consistent Boolean assignment to concrete theory values.

problems.q:

A) Theory conflict

B) Restart

C) Theory propagation

D) Bit-blasting
problems.a: Theory propagation
problems.e: Theory propagation sets implied atoms early, like unit propagation, with the theory providing the reason clause.

problems.q:
With x = y and y = z asserted, the EUF solver tells the SAT engine that atom x = z must be true before it is decided. What is this called?

A) Theory propagation

B) Bit-blasting

C) Restart

D) Theory conflict
problems.a: Theory propagation
problems.e: Theory propagation sets implied atoms early, like unit propagation, with the theory providing the reason clause.

problems.q:
The theory solver finds that x < 3 and x > 4 cannot both hold. What does it return to the SAT engine?

A) The explanation clause (¬b1 ∨ ¬b3), learned like a conflict clause

B) A request to restart

C) A satisfying assignment

D) The empty clause
problems.a: The explanation clause (¬b1 ∨ ¬b3), learned like a conflict clause
problems.e: A theory conflict is a set of literals that is inconsistent; its negation is a valid clause the SAT engine learns.

problems.q:
A bit-vector problem is solved by translating every operation into gates and clauses before search. Which style is this?

A) Lazy DPLL(T)

B) Eager: bit-blasting to SAT

C) Congruence closure

D) Nelson-Oppen combination
problems.a: Eager: bit-blasting to SAT
problems.e: Eager approaches translate the whole theory problem into propositional logic up front; lazy ones consult the theory during search.

problems.q:
Why do bit-vector solvers often simplify word-level terms before bit-blasting?

A) SAT solvers reject large formulas

B) Rewriting replaces the SAT engine

C) Bit-blasting is unsound without rewriting

D) Rewriting at the word level can remove whole operations, such as multiplications by constants, before they become thousands of clauses
problems.a: Rewriting at the word level can remove whole operations, such as multiplications by constants, before they become thousands of clauses
problems.e: Word-level preprocessing is far cheaper than solving the bit-level clauses it avoids.

problems.q:
A formula mixes linear integer arithmetic and uninterpreted functions. How does Nelson-Oppen combination let two theory solvers cooperate?

A) They bit-blast both theories

B) They share a single unique table

C) One solver runs after the other has finished

D) They exchange equalities between shared variables until both agree or one finds a conflict
problems.a: They exchange equalities between shared variables until both agree or one finds a conflict
problems.e: For stably infinite, signature-disjoint theories, propagating implied equalities between shared terms is enough to decide the combination.

label: Theorem proving for hardware
lesson:
# Theorem proving for hardware

Model checkers and SAT solvers decide questions about one finite design. Theorem provers prove statements about whole families of designs, such as an adder of every width or a processor against its instruction-set specification, at the price of human guidance. Several floating-point units and processor cores have been verified this way, and theorem provers also host the certified checkers that let other tools be trusted, so a tool designer should know when and how they are used.

## Interactive and automated provers

An interactive theorem prover checks proofs that a human structures with definitions, lemmas and tactics. Widely used systems include ACL2, HOL4, Isabelle/HOL, Coq (now Rocq) and Lean, all of which have been applied to hardware. Most follow the LCF approach: theorems are values of an abstract type that only a small trusted kernel of inference rules can create, so bugs in tactics or automation cannot produce false theorems. Automated provers, first-order resolution provers and SMT solvers, are called from inside interactive provers to discharge routine subgoals, and their results are either reconstructed in the kernel or trusted explicitly. The division of labor is the point: the human supplies the proof structure and the key invariants, and the machine checks every step and closes the easy goals.

## Proofs for every width

A model checker verifies one fixed design; an 8-bit adder and a 64-bit adder are different problems. A theorem prover can prove a parameterized statement for every width $n$ by induction. For a ripple-carry adder, the base case shows the 1-bit full adder computes $a + b + c_{in}$ as a 2-bit value; the inductive step shows that if the $n$-bit adder is correct, appending one full adder gives a correct $(n + 1)$-bit adder, because the carry out of the $n$-bit part has weight $2^n$. Processors are verified by refinement: an abstraction function maps pipelined states to architectural states, and the proof shows that every implementation step corresponds to zero or one specification steps. Proofs about compilers and synthesis passes use structural induction over the syntax tree, following the recursion that defines the pass.

## When to use a theorem prover

Theorem proving costs much more human effort than model checking, so it is used where automatic engines cannot reach: parameterized designs, deep arithmetic such as floating-point division and square root, cache-coherence protocols for any number of nodes, and full processor correctness. Most practical projects combine methods: the prover decomposes the problem and proves the general theorem, and SAT, BDD or model-checking engines discharge finite subproblems. Two cautions apply. A proof shows only that the design meets the stated specification, so a wrong specification gives a correct proof of the wrong thing; specifications are reviewed and tested for that reason. And every assumed axiom or unproved lemma joins the trusted base: a proof that relies on an assumed fact about rounding is only conditional until that fact is discharged.

## Going deeper

Kaufmann, Manolios and Moore, "Computer-Aided Reasoning: An Approach" (2000), on ACL2; Harrison, "Handbook of Practical Logic and Automated Reasoning" (2009); Russinoff, "Formal Verification of Floating-Point Hardware Design" (Springer).

problems.a: Every theorem is built through a small trusted kernel, so tactic bugs cannot produce false theorems
problems.e: Only the kernel's inference rules can create theorems; everything else is untrusted proof search.

label: Symbolic execution
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Symbolic execution

Symbolic execution runs a program, or an RTL model, on symbolic inputs instead of concrete ones. Each branch splits the run into paths, each path carries a path condition over the inputs, and an SMT solver decides which paths are feasible and produces inputs that drive them. It underlies test generation, bug finding and some hardware analysis tools, and its central problem, path explosion, is a counting problem.

## Paths through a program

A program with $k$ independent if-statements in sequence has $2^k$ syntactic paths: each branch can go either way, independently of the others. With three such statements there are 8 paths, with 30 over a billion. An if / else-if chain with $k$ conditions and a final else has only $k + 1$ paths, because exactly one arm executes. Loops multiply paths by the number of iterations considered, which is why symbolic executors bound loop unrolling. Hardware has the same structure: one clock cycle of an always_comb block with $k$ independent conditionals has $2^k$ paths, and $c$ cycles of symbolic simulation multiply them again. Counting syntactic paths is the first estimate of the cost, before the solver prunes any.

## Path conditions and feasibility

Along each path the executor collects a path condition: the conjunction of the branch conditions taken, each negated when the else side is taken. At each branch it asks an SMT solver whether the extended path condition is satisfiable; unsatisfiable paths are infeasible and pruned. Take a 4-bit unsigned input $x$ and the statements if ($x < 8$) ... ; if ($x \ge 12$) ... . The path that takes both branches needs $x < 8 \wedge x \ge 12$, which is unsatisfiable, so only 3 of the 4 syntactic paths are feasible. For small input domains the feasible paths are exactly the distinct branch-outcome patterns that some input produces, which can be counted by enumerating the inputs. A satisfying assignment of a feasible path condition is a concrete test input for that path, which is how symbolic executors generate tests.

## Counting the inputs on a path

The number of inputs that follow a path is the model count of its path condition. In the example, the path that takes neither branch has $\neg(x < 8) \wedge \neg(x \ge 12)$, so $8 \le x \le 11$: 4 inputs. Intersect the set allowed by each conjunct; for bit tests such as $x[0] = 1$, keep the values with that bit set. Model counts measure how likely a path is under random inputs, which explains why random testing misses rare paths and symbolic execution finds them. In practice, path explosion is managed by merging paths at join points into one state with ite expressions, by concolic execution (running concretely and negating one branch condition at a time), and by search heuristics that prioritize uncovered code. Tools such as KLEE apply these ideas to software, and symbolic simulation applies them to RTL.

## Going deeper

King, "Symbolic Execution and Program Testing" (Communications of the ACM, 1976); Cadar, Dunbar and Engler, "KLEE: Unassisted and Automatic Generation of High-Coverage Tests for Complex Systems Programs" (OSDI 2008).

label: Abstract interpretation with intervals
lesson:
# Abstract interpretation with intervals

Abstract interpretation computes sound over-approximations of all the values a program or design can produce, by running it over an abstract domain instead of concrete values. The interval domain, which tracks a lower and upper bound for each variable, is the simplest useful example. Compilers, static analyzers and HDL tools use it for range analysis, bit-width inference and dead-code detection, and the same lattice-and-fixpoint machinery underlies model checking.

## Interval arithmetic

Each variable is abstracted by an interval $[l, h]$ containing all its possible values, and each operation is replaced by a sound interval version. With $x \in [1, 3]$ and $y \in [-2, 4]$: $x + y \in [1 - 2, 3 + 4] = [-1, 7]$; $x - y \in [1 - 4, 3 + 2] = [-3, 5]$; and $x \cdot y$ takes the minimum and maximum of the four corner products $-2, 4, -6, 12$, so $[-6, 12]$. The results are sound, containing every concrete result, but can be imprecise. The classic loss is $x - x$, which interval arithmetic evaluates as $[1 - 3, 3 - 1] = [-2, 2]$ instead of $[0, 0]$, because the domain is non-relational: it forgets that both operands are the same variable. Relational domains such as octagons or polyhedra track constraints between variables and avoid this loss at higher cost.

## Joins at merge points

Where control flow merges, after an if-else or at a loop head, the analysis joins the intervals from each incoming path: $[a, b] \sqcup [c, d] = [\min(a, c), \max(b, d)]$, the smallest interval containing both. With $x \in [2, 5]$ and an unknown condition, if (c) x = x + 4; else x = x * 2 gives $[6, 9]$ on one side and $[4, 10]$ on the other, and the join is $[4, 10]$. The join loses information again: the analysis cannot express that $x$ is never 5, since intervals have no holes. The intervals ordered by inclusion form a lattice with this join, and every abstract operation is monotone, which is what guarantees that the analysis computes a sound fixpoint. Hardware tools use exactly this computation to infer that a signal never exceeds a bound and can be narrowed to fewer bits.

## Loops, fixpoints and widening

At a loop head the interval is the least fixpoint of: join of the entry value and the value coming around the loop. For i = 0; while (i < N) i = i + s, the body sees the head interval intersected with the guard $i \le N - 1$, and adds $s$. With $N = 10$ and $s = 3$, Kleene iteration gives head intervals $[0, 0]$, $[0, 3]$, $[0, 6]$, $[0, 9]$, then the clipped body $[0, 9] + 3 = [3, 12]$ makes the head $[0, 12]$, which is stable. In general the head stabilizes at $[0, N - 1 + s]$ and the exit interval, the head intersected with $i \ge N$, is $[N, N - 1 + s]$, here $[10, 12]$. Intervals cannot record that $i$ is a multiple of 3. For large $N$ this iteration takes $N / s$ steps, so analyzers apply widening, jumping an unstable bound to infinity to force termination, and then narrowing, which iterates downward to recover a finite bound such as 12.

## Going deeper

Cousot and Cousot, "Abstract Interpretation: A Unified Lattice Model for Static Analysis of Programs by Construction or Approximation of Fixpoints" (POPL 1977); Rival and Yi, "Introduction to Static Analysis: An Abstract Interpretation Perspective" (2020).

problems.e: The loop-head interval grows by 6 per iteration until the guard $i \le 7$ clips it; the clipped body yields at most 7 + 6 = 13, so the head stabilizes at $[0, 13]$ and the exit interval is $[8, 13]$. Intervals cannot record that i is a multiple of 6.

problems.q: Interval analysis without widening runs on: i = 0; while (i < 37) i = i + 7. At the fixpoint, what is the upper bound of the interval for i after the loop exits?
problems.e: The loop-head interval grows by 7 per iteration until the guard $i \le 36$ clips it; the clipped body yields at most 36 + 7 = 43, so the head stabilizes at $[0, 43]$ and the exit interval is $[37, 43]$. Intervals cannot record that i is a multiple of 7.

label: SystemVerilog assertions
lesson:
# SystemVerilog assertions

SystemVerilog assertions (SVA) are how hardware teams write temporal properties that both simulators and formal tools check. A concurrent assertion is sampled on a clock edge and, for an implication, starts a new attempt every cycle its antecedent holds. Counting failing and pending attempts on a waveform by hand is the quickest way to learn exactly what an assertion means, which is the first thing to get right before any proof.

## Overlapping and non-overlapping implication

assert property (@(posedge clk) a |-> b) samples the signals at each rising edge. At every cycle where the antecedent $a$ is 1, an attempt starts and checks the consequent: with the overlapping implication |->, $b$ must be 1 in the same cycle; with the non-overlapping implication |=>, $b$ must be 1 in the next cycle. Cycles where $a$ is 0 start no attempt and cannot fail. Take cycles 0 to 6 with $a$ = 0110100 and $b$ = 0011001, leftmost bit first. Attempts start at cycles 1, 2 and 4. For a |-> b, cycle 1 fails ($b = 0$), cycle 2 passes and cycle 4 fails: 2 failures. For a |=> b, cycle 1 checks $b$ at 2 (passes), cycle 2 checks cycle 3 (passes) and cycle 4 checks cycle 5 (fails): 1 failure. An attempt whose check cycle lies beyond the end of a finite trace is pending, neither passed nor failed.

## Fixed delays

The cycle delay ##n moves the check $n$ cycles forward: a |-> ##2 b requires $b$ exactly two cycles after each cycle where $a$ holds, and a |=> b is the same as a |-> ##1 b. With the trace above, $a$ = 0110100 and $b$ = 0011001, the attempts at cycles 1, 2 and 4 check $b$ at cycles 3, 4 and 6: 1, 0 and 1. So one attempt fails, the one started at cycle 2. If $a$ were also 1 at cycle 5, that attempt would need $b$ at cycle 7, beyond a 7-cycle trace, and would be pending. In simulation, pending attempts at the end of a test are usually reported separately; in formal verification there is no end of trace, and BMC only reports an assertion as failing when a complete failing attempt fits within its bound.

## Delay ranges

A range ##[m:n] lets the consequent happen at any cycle from $m$ to $n$ cycles after the antecedent: a |-> ##[1:3] b passes as soon as $b$ is seen in that window and fails only when the whole window passes without $b$. Take cycles 0 to 7 with $a$ = 10111000 and $b$ = 00011000 and the property a |-> ##[1:2] b. The attempt at cycle 0 checks cycles 1 and 2, both 0: fail. The attempt at 2 sees $b$ at 3: pass. The attempt at 3 sees $b$ at 4: pass. The attempt at 4 checks cycles 5 and 6, both 0: fail. Two failures. An attempt whose window is cut off by the end of the trace passes if $b$ already appeared and is pending otherwise. Unbounded ranges, whose upper end is written with a dollar sign, describe liveness, and their formal treatment differs.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800 (SystemVerilog), the chapter on assertions; Cerny, Dudani, Havlicek and Korchemny, "SVA: The Power of Assertions in SystemVerilog" (2nd ed., 2015).

label: SVA sequences and repetition
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# SVA sequences and repetition

SVA properties are built from sequences: patterns of signal values over consecutive cycles, joined by cycle delays and repetitions. Sampled-value functions compare a signal with its value in the previous cycle. Counting where a sequence matches on a trace is how you check that a property says what you mean, and the same matching semantics is what formal tools compile into automata or monitor circuits.

## Sampled-value functions

The system functions rose, fell and stable (each written with a leading dollar sign in SVA source) compare the value of a signal sampled at the current clock edge with the value sampled at the previous edge. rose(a) is true when $a$ goes from 0 to 1, fell(a) when it goes from 1 to 0, and stable(a) when it is unchanged. At the first sample there is no previous one, so a starting value must be assumed; in this course it is 0. Take $a$ = 0110 on cycles 0 to 3. rose(a) is true at cycle 1; fell(a) at cycle 3; stable(a) at cycle 0 (0 against the assumed 0) and cycle 2 (1 against 1), so twice. These functions express edge-triggered protocol rules, for example \"after rose(req), req stays high until ack\", without extra registers in the RTL.

## Concatenation with cycle delays

The sequence a ##1 b matches starting at cycle $t$ if $a$ is 1 at $t$ and $b$ is 1 at $t + 1$; a ##2 b requires $b$ at $t + 2$ with any value in between; a ##1 b ##1 c needs $a$, $b$ and $c$ on three consecutive cycles. To count matching start cycles, slide the pattern along the trace and require it to end within the trace. With $a$ = 01110110000 and $b$ = 01001011111 (cycles 0 to 10), a ##1 b matches where $a[t] = 1$ and $b[t + 1] = 1$. $a$ is 1 at cycles 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6; $b$ at the next cycle is 0, 0, 1, 1 and 1. So matches start at cycles 3, 5 and 6: 3 matches. In an implication such as s |-> p, every start cycle where $s$ matches launches an attempt of $p$.

## Consecutive repetition

b[*2] means $b$ on two consecutive cycles, and b[*1:2] means one or two consecutive cycles of $b$; so a ##1 b[*2] ##1 c needs $a$ at $t$, $b$ at $t + 1$ and $t + 2$, and $c$ at $t + 3$. A range creates several possible matches from one start: a ##1 b[*1:2] ##1 c matches from $t$ if either $b$ at $t + 1$ and $c$ at $t + 2$, or $b$ at $t + 1$ and $t + 2$ and $c$ at $t + 3$. Count a start cycle once if at least one alternative matches within the trace. With $a$ = 100100, $b$ = 011010 and $c$ = 000101: from cycle 0, $b$ at 1 and 2, then $c$ at 3 matches the two-repetition branch; from cycle 3, $b$ at 4 then $c$ at 5 matches the one-repetition branch. Two start cycles match. Formal tools turn each such sequence into a small automaton whose states track the partial matches.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800 (SystemVerilog), the chapter on assertions; Cerny, Dudani, Havlicek and Korchemny, "SVA: The Power of Assertions in SystemVerilog" (2nd ed., 2015).
