label: Assume, assert and cover
lesson:
# Assume, assert and cover

A formal testbench has three kinds of directive. Assertions state what the design must do and are proved. Assumptions state what the environment does and are trusted. Covers ask whether something can happen and return a witness trace. Getting the balance right is what separates a meaningful proof from one that passes for trivial reasons, so this is the most important methodology concept in property checking.

## Three directives, three jobs

assert property (p) asks the tool to prove that $p$ holds on every trace allowed by the assumptions, or to return a counterexample. assume property (q) restricts the traces the tool considers: inputs are chosen only in ways that satisfy $q$, so assumptions encode the interface contract, such as \"the sender never asserts valid during reset\". cover property (r) asks for one trace on which $r$ happens and returns it as a witness. Every counterexample obeys every assumption, so a counterexample is always a legal environment behavior. The same property can play different roles in different proofs: in assume-guarantee reasoning, block A asserts a property about its outputs and block B, which consumes them, assumes it. The composition is sound only when every assumed property is proved somewhere.

## Over-constraining assumptions

Assumptions are not checked, so a wrong one silently removes behaviors from the proof. The extreme case is a contradiction: if the assumptions cannot all hold on any trace after reset, there are no traces at all, and every assertion passes vacuously. A milder case is common: an engineer adds assume property (!req) to silence a confusing counterexample, and the design now never receives a request, so its assertions pass while saying almost nothing. Even a correct-looking assumption can be false in silicon, for example if the real sender can raise valid during reset; then the proofs do not cover the real behavior. The defenses are to keep assumptions few and traceable to the interface specification, to prove them as assertions on the block that drives those signals, and to check them with covers.

## Covers and vacuity

An implication with an antecedent that can never be true passes vacuously: req |-> ##[1:3] ack is proved if req is stuck at 0. The guard is a cover on the antecedent, cover property (req), which must be reachable. More generally, teams write covers for the normal behaviors a block must exhibit, such as a full FIFO, a back-to-back transfer or a retry; a reached cover returns a witness trace, useful for sanity checks and waveform review, and an unreachable cover flags either dead logic or assumptions that exclude legal behavior. Cover mode in tools such as SymbiYosys searches for these witnesses directly. A proof is trustworthy only when its key covers are reached under the same assumptions, so in practice every significant assertion comes with at least one cover.

## Going deeper

Cerny, Dudani, Havlicek and Korchemny, "SVA: The Power of Assertions in SystemVerilog" (2nd ed., 2015); Seligman, Schubert and Kumar, "Formal Verification: An Essential Toolkit for Modern VLSI Design" (2nd ed., 2023).

problems.q:
A block's spec says the upstream sender never asserts valid while reset is high. In a formal testbench for the block, which directive states this?

A) restrict nothing and rely on simulation

B) assume property

C) assert property

D) cover property
problems.a: assume property
problems.e: Facts about the environment are assumptions: they limit the inputs the prover may choose.

problems.q:
The prover reports an assertion as failing. What does it hand back?

A) A trace from reset that obeys every assumption and violates the assertion

B) A proof certificate

C) A coverage percentage

D) A list of assumptions to remove
problems.a: A trace from reset that obeys every assumption and violates the assertion
problems.e: Counterexamples always respect the assumptions, which is why a wrong assumption can hide bugs.

problems.q:
A block's spec says the upstream sender never asserts valid while reset is high. In a formal testbench for the block, which directive states this?

A) restrict nothing and rely on simulation

B) assume property

C) cover property

D) assert property
problems.a: assume property
problems.e: Facts about the environment are assumptions: they limit the inputs the prover may choose.

problems.q:
How can a team detect that assumptions are over-constraining?

A) Write covers for expected behaviors and check that each one is reachable

B) Remove every assertion

C) Run BMC with a smaller depth

D) Turn assumptions into comments
problems.a: Write covers for expected behaviors and check that each one is reachable
problems.e: If a cover of normal operation becomes unreachable, the assumptions have excluded it.

problems.q:
A designer adds assume property (!req) to silence a confusing counterexample. All assertions now pass. What is the danger?

A) The proof becomes slower

B) Nothing: assumptions are checked like assertions

C) The assertions become covers

D) With req never asserted, the design never does anything, so the passes are meaningless
problems.a: With req never asserted, the design never does anything, so the passes are meaningless
problems.e: Over-constraining assumptions remove the behaviors where bugs live; the proof is sound but says almost nothing.

problems.q:
Two assumptions contradict each other in every state reachable after reset. What happens to all assertions?

A) Only assertions that mention the assumed signals pass

B) They all pass vacuously, because no trace satisfies the assumptions

C) The tool reports a syntax error

D) They all fail
problems.a: They all pass vacuously, because no trace satisfies the assumptions
problems.e: If no trace obeys the assumptions, there is no counterexample to any assertion, so everything trivially passes.

problems.q:
A cover property stays unreachable after an unbounded proof. Which conclusions are possible?

A) The state is truly unreachable, or the assumptions exclude it; both need review

B) The cover passed

C) The prover timed out

D) The design certainly has a bug
problems.a: The state is truly unreachable, or the assumptions exclude it; both need review
problems.e: Unreachable covers flag either dead logic or over-constrained environments.

problems.q:
Which cover catches the vacuity of req |-> ##[1:3] ack?

A) assert property (ack)

B) assume property (req)

C) cover property (!ack)

D) cover property (req)
problems.a: cover property (req)
problems.e: Covering the antecedent shows that the implication is actually exercised.

problems.q:
Which cover catches the vacuity of req |-> ##[1:3] ack?

A) assume property (req)

B) cover property (req)

C) cover property (!ack)

D) assert property (ack)
problems.a: cover property (req)
problems.e: Covering the antecedent shows that the implication is actually exercised.

label: Formal apps: X-propagation, connectivity and CDC
lesson:
# Formal apps: X-propagation, connectivity and CDC

Formal apps package property checking for specific, recurring questions, so that engineers who never write a temporal property still get exhaustive answers. The properties are generated from a specification or from the design's structure, and the engines underneath are the BMC, induction and IC3 engines of this domain. X-propagation, connectivity and clock-domain-crossing checks are three of the most widely used.

## X-propagation checks

Registers without reset start with unknown values, and RTL simulation represents them as X. Simulation is unreliable about X: an if statement whose condition is X takes the else branch, which can hide the fact that real hardware might go either way, while other constructs can propagate X pessimistically. A formal X-propagation app instead treats every unknown bit as a free value and asks whether a signal that should always be known, such as a control output or a valid-qualified data bus, can differ between two resolutions of the unknowns. Technically this is a miter: two copies of the design with the same inputs and independent initial values, compared at the checked points. A difference is reported with a trace; no difference proves the X harmless. Checks are written relative to qualifiers: unknown data under a low valid bit is usually by design.

## Connectivity checking

SoC integration wires thousands of signals between IP blocks: interrupts, resets, clocks, debug and test buses. A connectivity app reads a connection specification, often a spreadsheet, and turns each row into a property: the destination equals the source, possibly after a fixed number of register stages, and possibly only when a condition holds, such as test_mode == 0 or a mux select set to a given value. Each check involves only the cone of logic between two points, a few muxes, buffers and flops, so it is fast even on a full chip. Formal search explores every configuration, including debug and test modes that directed simulation rarely sets, so a failing check often reveals a path where some unrelated register can override a connection that the specification says is fixed.

## Clock-domain crossing formal

Signals crossing between asynchronous clock domains can go metastable. Structural CDC analysis finds every crossing and checks that it uses an approved synchronizer, typically two flip-flops in the destination domain with no combinational logic in between. Formal CDC goes further and checks functional rules. A multi-bit value synchronized bit by bit is safe only if at most one bit changes per source cycle, as with gray-coded FIFO pointers, which is an assertion on the source logic. Two synchronized bits that reconverge downstream can resolve in different cycles and briefly form an illegal combination. To check that the design tolerates synchronizer uncertainty, formal tools inject metastability effects, a random extra cycle of latency or a random value at each synchronizer, and re-run the functional properties. Metastability itself cannot be proved away; the checks show that its consequences are contained.

## Going deeper

Seligman, Schubert and Kumar, "Formal Verification: An Essential Toolkit for Modern VLSI Design" (2nd ed., 2023); Cummings, "Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) Design and Verification Techniques Using SystemVerilog" (SNUG 2008).

problems.q:
A datapath register has no reset, and an X check reports that the X reaches a valid-qualified output only while valid is 0. Is that a bug?

A) No, X values never matter

B) Yes, every X on an output is a bug

C) Usually not: the data is don't-care while valid is low

D) Yes, the register must be reset
problems.a: Usually not: the data is don't-care while valid is low
problems.e: X checks are written relative to qualifying conditions; unknown data under an invalid flag is often by design.

problems.q:
Why can RTL simulation be optimistic about X values?

A) An if statement treats an X condition as false and takes the else branch, hiding that real hardware could go either way

B) X values never reach registers in simulation

C) Simulation always propagates X pessimistically

D) Simulators convert X to 1
problems.a: An if statement treats an X condition as false and takes the else branch, hiding that real hardware could go either way
problems.e: Verilog's if semantics resolve X to a single branch, so simulation can show a clean value where silicon is unknown.

problems.q:
A datapath register has no reset, and an X check reports that the X reaches a valid-qualified output only while valid is 0. Is that a bug?

A) Yes, the register must be reset

B) Usually not: the data is don't-care while valid is low

C) Yes, every X on an output is a bug

D) No, X values never matter
problems.a: Usually not: the data is don't-care while valid is low
problems.e: X checks are written relative to qualifying conditions; unknown data under an invalid flag is often by design.

problems.q:
A connectivity property fails with a trace that sets an unrelated debug register. What did the check find?

A) A missing clock

B) A timing violation

C) A vacuous proof

D) A path where the debug logic can override the connection, which the spec did not allow
problems.a: A path where the debug logic can override the connection, which the spec did not allow
problems.e: Formal search explores every configuration, including debug modes that directed tests rarely set.

problems.q:
An SoC integration team wants to prove that 400 interrupt lines are wired from the right IP outputs to the right controller inputs. Which app fits?

A) X-propagation analysis

B) Formal connectivity checking against a connection specification

C) CDC structural analysis

D) Combinational equivalence of the IPs
problems.a: Formal connectivity checking against a connection specification
problems.e: Connectivity apps turn each spreadsheet row into a property such as "source equals destination, possibly after a fixed delay or when a mux select is set".

problems.q:
An SoC integration team wants to prove that 400 interrupt lines are wired from the right IP outputs to the right controller inputs. Which app fits?

A) X-propagation analysis

B) Formal connectivity checking against a connection specification

C) CDC structural analysis

D) Combinational equivalence of the IPs
problems.a: Formal connectivity checking against a connection specification
problems.e: Connectivity apps turn each spreadsheet row into a property such as "source equals destination, possibly after a fixed delay or when a mux select is set".

problems.q:
A single bit crosses from clock domain A to clock domain B through two flip-flops in B. What does a structural CDC check confirm?

A) That the bit never goes metastable

B) That the data is gray coded

C) That the clocks are related

D) That a synchronizer is present and nothing combinational sits between the domains
problems.a: That a synchronizer is present and nothing combinational sits between the domains
problems.e: Structural CDC finds crossings and checks their synchronizer structure; it cannot remove metastability, only bound its consequences.

problems.q:
A multi-bit counter value crosses clock domains through per-bit synchronizers. Which formal property makes this safe?

A) The counter is one-hot

B) The destination clock is faster

C) Each bit has its own reset

D) The value is gray coded: at most one bit changes per source clock cycle
problems.a: The value is gray coded: at most one bit changes per source clock cycle
problems.e: If several bits can change at once, the destination may capture a mix of old and new bits; gray coding limits the change to one bit.

problems.q:
A single bit crosses from clock domain A to clock domain B through two flip-flops in B. What does a structural CDC check confirm?

A) That the clocks are related

B) That the bit never goes metastable

C) That a synchronizer is present and nothing combinational sits between the domains

D) That the data is gray coded
problems.a: That a synchronizer is present and nothing combinational sits between the domains
problems.e: Structural CDC finds crossings and checks their synchronizer structure; it cannot remove metastability, only bound its consequences.

label: SymbiYosys and open formal tools
lesson:
# SymbiYosys and open formal tools

SymbiYosys (sby) is the open-source front end for formal hardware verification built on Yosys. It reads a short configuration file, runs Yosys to turn the design and its properties into a formal model, and dispatches the model to engines such as yosys-smtbmc and ABC. Knowing its file format, modes and engines is the practical way into every concept of this domain, because each engine corresponds to an algorithm studied here.

## The .sby file

A .sby file is divided into sections. [options] sets the mode, for example mode prove, and parameters such as depth 20. [engines] lists one or more engines to run. [script] holds the Yosys commands that read and prepare the design, typically read -formal for each source file, which enables the assert, assume and cover constructs, followed by prep -top with the top module's name. [files] lists the source files to copy into the run directory. An optional [tasks] section names several configurations, such as bmc and prove, and option lines prefixed with a task name apply only to that task, so one file can drive a bounded bug hunt and an unbounded proof of the same design. Results land in a directory per task, with a status file and trace files.

## Modes and engines

Modes select the question. bmc checks the assertions up to the depth. prove tries to establish them for all depths. cover searches for traces that reach each cover statement. live checks liveness properties with engines that support them. Engines select the algorithm. smtbmc drives an SMT solver, for example smtbmc yices, smtbmc boolector or smtbmc z3; in prove mode it runs k-induction, a BMC base case plus an induction step of the configured depth, both of which must pass. abc pdr runs ABC's IC3 implementation, which builds an inductive invariant itself and often succeeds where k-induction's step keeps failing. abc bmc3 is ABC's incremental bounded model checker. Several engines can be listed, and the first conclusive answer wins, which is a simple portfolio strategy.

## Reading the results

PASS in bmc mode means no assertion fails within the depth, not forever. FAIL comes with a counterexample trace, written as a VCD waveform and often as a testbench, that starts at reset and obeys all assumptions. In prove mode with smtbmc, a failing base case is a real bug, while a passing base case with a failing induction step produces an induction trace that starts from an arbitrary state satisfying the assertions for $k$ cycles; it is a counterexample to induction, usually fixed by a helper assertion or a larger depth, not by changing the RTL. A cover run reports each cover as reached, with a witness trace, or unreached. When a failing trace shows inputs the real environment never produces, the fix is an assume statement describing the legal behavior.

## Going deeper

The SymbiYosys documentation (YosysHQ); the Yosys manual, the chapters on formal verification and the write_smt2 and write_aiger backends; the ABC documentation for pdr and bmc3.

problems.q:
A .sby file has a [tasks] section listing bmc and prove. What does that allow?

A) Running two designs at once

B) Running the same setup in several configurations, each task selecting its own options

C) Merging BMC and induction into one solver call

D) Skipping the [script] section
problems.a: Running the same setup in several configurations, each task selecting its own options
problems.e: Tasks let one file describe several runs, with option lines prefixed by task names.

problems.q:
What does the Yosys command read -formal do that a plain read does not?

A) It enables the formal constructs (assert, assume, cover) in the Verilog front end

B) It runs the SAT solver

C) It synthesizes the design to gates

D) It writes the .sby file
problems.a: It enables the formal constructs (assert, assume, cover) in the Verilog front end
problems.e: read -formal parses the design with formal verification features enabled so the properties become part of the netlist.

problems.q:
In a SymbiYosys .sby file, which section holds the Yosys commands that read and prepare the design?

A) [engines]

B) [files]

C) [options]

D) [script]
problems.a: [script]
problems.e: [script] lists commands such as read -formal and prep -top; [files] lists the source files to copy into the work directory.

problems.q:
An induction step keeps failing with smtbmc even at large depths. Which engine line offers a different kind of unbounded proof?

A) abc bmc3

B) smtbmc yices with a larger depth

C) abc sim3

D) abc pdr
problems.a: abc pdr
problems.e: abc pdr runs ABC's IC3 implementation, which builds its own inductive invariant instead of relying on k-induction.

problems.q:
An induction step keeps failing with smtbmc even at large depths. Which engine line offers a different kind of unbounded proof?

A) abc bmc3

B) smtbmc yices with a larger depth

C) abc sim3

D) abc pdr
problems.a: abc pdr
problems.e: abc pdr runs ABC's IC3 implementation, which builds its own inductive invariant instead of relying on k-induction.

problems.q:
Which mode asks SymbiYosys for an unbounded proof of the assertions?

A) sim

B) bmc

C) cover

D) prove
problems.a: prove
problems.e: bmc checks up to the depth, cover looks for witness traces, and prove tries to establish the assertions for all depths.

problems.q:
A bmc run with depth 20 passes. What has been established?

A) No assertion can fail within 20 cycles of reset

B) The assertions are inductive

C) The assertions hold forever

D) Every cover is reachable
problems.a: No assertion can fail within 20 cycles of reset
problems.e: BMC is bounded; only prove mode (or a completeness argument) extends the result to all depths.

problems.q:
A prove run reports that the base case passed and the induction step failed. What does that trace show?

A) A vacuous assertion

B) A syntax error in the .sby file

C) A counterexample to induction, which may start in an unreachable state

D) A real bug reachable from reset
problems.a: A counterexample to induction, which may start in an unreachable state
problems.e: The induction trace starts from an arbitrary state satisfying the assertions for k steps, so it often needs a helper assertion, not a design fix.

problems.q:
A cover run finishes with every cover reached. What files are most useful to look at?

A) The synthesized gate netlist

B) The witness traces (VCD waveforms) produced for each cover

C) The solver's learned clauses

D) The induction traces
problems.a: The witness traces (VCD waveforms) produced for each cover
problems.e: Each reached cover has a trace showing how the design gets there, which is the point of cover mode.

label: Agent-proposed invariants filtered by the prover
lesson:
# Agent-proposed invariants filtered by the prover

Unbounded proofs often stall for lack of a strengthening invariant, and proposing candidate invariants is exactly the kind of guess a language model or agent can make cheaply. The formal engine then filters the guesses. The Houdini algorithm does this filtering with nothing but induction checks: start from all candidates and repeatedly drop the ones that are not inductive relative to the rest. Whatever survives is sound by construction, so the proposer never needs to be trusted.

## Candidates in, survivors out

An agent proposes candidate invariants $c_1, \dots, c_m$, each a set of states (in practice, an assertion over the design's signals). Houdini looks for the largest subset whose conjunction is inductive. One round works as follows: let $\text{Inv}$ be the conjunction (intersection) of all surviving candidates; remove every candidate that fails initiation (excludes an initial state) or that some state of $\text{Inv}$ can leave in one transition, $\text{Inv} \wedge T \not\rightarrow c'$. Example: states s0 to s3, initial s0, transitions s0 → s1, s1 → s0, s1 → s2, s2 → s0; candidates $c_1 = \{s0, s1, s2, s3\}$, $c_2 = \{s0, s1\}$, $c_3 = \{s0\}$. In round 1, $\text{Inv} = \{s0\}$, whose only successor s1 is outside $c_3$, so $c_3$ is removed, while $c_1$ and $c_2$ survive: 2 candidates.

## Iterating to the fixpoint

Removing a candidate weakens the conjunction, so a state that was excluded before may now be inside $\text{Inv}$, and its successors can break another candidate. So Houdini repeats rounds until one removes nothing. In the example, round 2 has $\text{Inv} = c_1 \cap c_2 = \{s0, s1\}$; s1 now steps to s2, which $c_2$ excludes, so $c_2$ is removed. Round 3 has $\text{Inv} = c_1$, all states, every successor stays inside $c_1$, and nothing is removed. One candidate survives. At the fixpoint, initiation holds and $\text{Inv} \wedge T \rightarrow c'$ for every survivor, so $\text{Inv} \wedge T \rightarrow \text{Inv}'$: the conjunction of the survivors is an inductive invariant, and it is the largest inductive subset of the candidates. If it implies the target property, the property is proved; otherwise the agent proposes more candidates and the loop continues.

## Rounds, cost and trust

Each round costs one SAT query per surviving candidate (or one query with activation literals for all of them), and each round except the last removes at least one candidate, so there are at most $m + 1$ rounds for $m$ candidates; the example used 3, counting the final round that removes nothing. Two properties make this a good fit for agents. Soundness does not depend on the proposer: a wrong candidate is simply removed, so an agent can propose hundreds of guesses, including hallucinated or irrelevant ones, and the prover keeps only what is true together. And failures are informative: a removed candidate comes with a counterexample to induction that the agent can read to propose a better one. The cost to watch is the number of candidates, since every bad guess costs solver time, and a seed set of mutually supporting good candidates matters more than volume.

## Going deeper

Flanagan and Leino, "Houdini, an Annotation Assistant for ESC/Java" (FME 2001); Bradley, "SAT-Based Model Checking without Unrolling" (VMCAI 2011), on inductive strengthening.

problems.q: An agent proposes candidate invariants for a system with states s0 to s7, initial state s0 and transitions s0 → s2; s1 → s2, s5; s2 → s3; s3 → s6; s4 → s5, s6; s5 → s3; s6 → s0, s6; s7 → s1, s6. Candidates (each is the set of states it allows): c1 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6}; c2 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7}; c3 = {s0, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7}; c4 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s5, s6, s7}. problems.q: An agent proposes candidate invariants for a system with states s0 to s7, initial state s0 and transitions s0 → s3, s7; s1 → s5; s2 → s0, s1; s3 → s4, s5; s4 → s2, s5; s5 → s6; s6 → s7; s7 → s5. Candidates (each is the set of states it allows): c1 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s5, s6, s7}; c2 = {s0, s4, s5, s6, s7}; c3 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s7}; c4 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7}; c5 = {s0, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6}. Houdini runs rounds: it takes the conjunction (intersection) of all surviving candidates, and removes every candidate that excludes s0 or that some state of the conjunction can leave in one transition; it repeats until a round removes nothing. How many rounds run, counting the final round that removes nothing?
problems.e: Rounds keep removing candidates until the survivors' conjunction is inductive; that takes 3 rounds including the last, empty one, ending with 1 survivors.

problems.q: An agent proposes candidate invariants for a system with states s0 to s7, initial state s0 and transitions s0 → s0, s6; s1 → s7; s2 → s3, s5; s3 → s0; s4 → s0, s2; s5 → s0; s6 → s2, s7; s7 → s5. Candidates (each is the set of states it allows): c1 = {s0, s1, s2, s5, s7}; c2 = {s0, s1, s2, s5, s6, s7}; c3 = {s0, s1, s3, s4, s5, s7}; c4 = {s0, s3, s5, s7}; c5 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7}; c6 = {s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7}. Houdini runs rounds: it takes the conjunction (intersection) of all surviving candidates, and removes every candidate that excludes s0 or that some state of the conjunction can leave in one transition; it repeats until a round removes nothing. How many rounds run, counting the final round that removes nothing?
problems.e: Rounds keep removing candidates until the survivors' conjunction is inductive; that takes 3 rounds including the last, empty one, ending with 2 survivors.

label: Checking machine-written SVA with the prover
lesson:
# Checking machine-written SVA with the prover

Language models can turn specifications into SystemVerilog assertions quickly, but a generated assertion can be malformed, vacuous, trivially true or simply wrong. The formal engine is the gate that decides which generated properties are kept. A good harness runs a staged series of deterministic checks, from parsing to mutation testing, and feeds every failure back to the model, so that the human only reviews properties that have already earned their place.

## Syntax and elaboration gates

The cheapest checks come first. Parse each generated property, elaborate it against the RTL, and reject anything with syntax errors, unknown signals, width mismatches or constructs the formal tool ignores or rewrites; warnings count as failures, because a construct the tool silently changes no longer means what the model intended. These checks are fast, deterministic and precise, so their messages make excellent feedback for the model's next attempt, in the edit-check loop of an agent harness. Generated properties live in a separate bind file or checker module, not in the RTL, so the design under test is untouched and the change sits at the smallest change tier, easy to review and revert. Only properties that elaborate cleanly move on to the prover, which keeps expensive solver time for candidates that are at least well formed.

## Vacuity and covers

A proved assertion is not yet a useful one. An implication whose antecedent never fires passes vacuously, so the harness covers the antecedent of every generated implication and discards or flags properties whose cover is unreachable. Generated assumptions need more scrutiny than generated assertions, because assumptions are trusted: a wrong one can make every assertion pass by removing behaviors. So the harness keeps a fixed, human-reviewed set of covers for normal operation, such as a completed transfer or a full FIFO, and rejects any generated assumption under which one of them becomes unreachable. Generated assumptions about a block's inputs should also be proved as assertions on the block that drives them. Properties that pass, are non-vacuous and leave the reference covers reachable go on to the last filter, which asks whether they constrain anything at all.

## Does the assertion have teeth

A property can be non-vacuous and still useless, for example a register compared with itself one cycle later when it never changes. Mutation testing measures strength: inject small faults into the RTL (flip a comparison, drop an enable, swap two mux inputs), re-run the prover, and count how many mutants each property kills, that is, makes fail. A property set that passes on the real design and kills most mutants constrains real behavior; surviving mutants point to behavior no property covers, unless the mutation was functionally equivalent. When an expert reference property exists, the harness can check equivalence formally: build both properties as monitors on the same design and prove their verdicts always agree, a miter of two monitors. Throughout, the model proposes and the prover disposes: verdicts come from sound, checkable engines, never from the model's own confidence.

## Going deeper

Claessen, "A Coverage Analysis for Safety Property Lists" (FMCAD 2007); Seligman, Schubert and Kumar, "Formal Verification: An Essential Toolkit for Modern VLSI Design" (2nd ed., 2023), on vacuity and coverage.

problems.q:
A generated property compiles but uses a blocking delay construct that the formal tool ignores. How should the harness treat tool warnings?

A) As successes

B) As passes after one retry

C) As failures to report back to the model, since a silently ignored construct changes the meaning

D) As covers
problems.a: As failures to report back to the model, since a silently ignored construct changes the meaning
problems.e: A property whose meaning the tool changed cannot be trusted; warnings are part of the deterministic feedback.

problems.q:
A language model writes 200 SVA properties from a spec. What is the cheapest first filter before any proof?

A) Prove every property with IC3

B) Parse and elaborate each property against the RTL, rejecting syntax errors and unknown signals

C) Ask the model whether each property is correct

D) Simulate each property for a million cycles
problems.a: Parse and elaborate each property against the RTL, rejecting syntax errors and unknown signals
problems.e: Front-end checks are fast and deterministic, and they remove a large share of broken output before expensive engines run.

problems.q:
A language model writes 200 SVA properties from a spec. What is the cheapest first filter before any proof?

A) Parse and elaborate each property against the RTL, rejecting syntax errors and unknown signals

B) Ask the model whether each property is correct

C) Prove every property with IC3

D) Simulate each property for a million cycles
problems.a: Parse and elaborate each property against the RTL, rejecting syntax errors and unknown signals
problems.e: Front-end checks are fast and deterministic, and they remove a large share of broken output before expensive engines run.

problems.q:
A model proposes assume properties along with assertions. Why does that need extra scrutiny?

A) A wrong assumption can make every assertion pass by removing behaviors

B) Assumptions only matter in simulation

C) Assumptions are slower to prove

D) Assumptions cannot be generated
problems.a: A wrong assumption can make every assertion pass by removing behaviors
problems.e: Assumptions are trusted, not checked, so generated ones must be reviewed or proved on the neighboring block.

problems.q:
Many generated assertions pass, and every one of their antecedents is covered. What else could still make them weak?

A) They may have been too slow

B) They may state something trivially true of the design, such as a register equal to itself one cycle later when it never changes

C) They may be syntax errors

D) Nothing: covered and proved means strong
problems.a: They may state something trivially true of the design, such as a register equal to itself one cycle later when it never changes
problems.e: Non-vacuous is not the same as useful; checking that a property can fail on a broken design is the next filter.

problems.q:
A generated assertion a |-> b proves immediately. What should the harness check before counting it?

A) That the model is confident

B) That b is a primary output

C) That the proof took longer than a second

D) That a cover on the antecedent a is reachable, so the proof is not vacuous
problems.a: That a cover on the antecedent a is reachable, so the proof is not vacuous
problems.e: An assertion whose antecedent can never fire passes for trivial reasons.

problems.q:
A generated assertion is meant to match a reference assertion written by an expert. How can a prover check that they are equivalent?

A) Simulate one random test

B) Ask the model to compare them

C) Build both as monitors on the same design and prove that their outputs are always equal, like a miter

D) Compare the two texts
problems.a: Build both as monitors on the same design and prove that their outputs are always equal, like a miter
problems.e: Two monitor automata are equivalent if no trace makes one fail and the other pass, which is a formal check.

problems.q:
Why is the prover, not the language model, the authority on whether a generated property holds?

A) The prover is faster at reading specs

B) Provers never time out

C) The model cannot write SVA

D) The prover's answer is a sound, checkable result, while the model's opinion is not
problems.a: The prover's answer is a sound, checkable result, while the model's opinion is not
problems.e: The model proposes and the prover disposes: proofs and counterexamples can be checked independently.

problems.q:
A generated assertion is meant to match a reference assertion written by an expert. How can a prover check that they are equivalent?

A) Ask the model to compare them

B) Simulate one random test

C) Compare the two texts

D) Build both as monitors on the same design and prove that their outputs are always equal, like a miter
problems.a: Build both as monitors on the same design and prove that their outputs are always equal, like a miter
problems.e: Two monitor automata are equivalent if no trace makes one fail and the other pass, which is a formal check.

label: Counterexample-guided agent repair
lesson:
# Counterexample-guided agent repair

When a property fails, the prover returns a counterexample trace, which is unusually good input for an agent: short, precise and reproducible. An agentic repair loop reads the trace, localizes the cause, proposes a fix to the RTL, the environment model or the property, and re-runs the proofs. The engineering problem is making that loop trustworthy: the checks must be fixed, the edits tiered, and weakening the specification must never count as a repair.

## Reading the counterexample

BMC deepens one cycle at a time, so its first counterexample is a shortest one, with few irrelevant cycles. The agent first extracts the failing cycle and the signals in the assertion's cone of influence leading up to it, which turns a large waveform into a handful of events. Then it classifies the trace. A base-case trace from reset is a real failure of the design or of the environment model. A trace that drives inputs the interface specification forbids points to a missing assumption, not a design bug. An induction-step trace starts from an arbitrary state satisfying the assertions, so it may begin in an unreachable state and call for a helper invariant rather than an RTL change. Getting this classification right decides which artifact the fix should touch, and it is checkable: BMC aimed at the trace's start state tells whether that state is reachable.

## Proposing and checking a fix

The agent proposes a small edit and the harness re-runs the checks. The target assertion must now hold, and every previously passing assertion and cover must still pass: the whole property suite is the differential check against regressions, just as golden tests are for engine changes. A new counterexample is fed back as feedback for the next attempt. Covers matter here: a fix that makes a handshake assertion pass by stalling the interface forever satisfies every safety property and breaks the design, and a cover for normal traffic catches it. Bounded passes are not the end: if the original bug appeared at depth 14, BMC to depth 30 is evidence, not proof, so the loop should finish with an unbounded proof by k-induction or IC3 where one is achievable, and report the strength of the evidence when it is not.

## Guardrails on the repair loop

Some edits make failures disappear without fixing anything. Widening req |-> ##[1:2] ack to req |-> ##[1:200] ack, deleting an assertion or adding an assume that rules out the counterexample's inputs all weaken the specification. An assumption is legitimate only if the interface specification really forbids the behavior and the assumption is proved on the driving block. So the harness keeps the property suite, the covers and the assumptions under human control, outside the agent's edit scope, and runs in a sandbox that the agent cannot use to change its own oracle. Edits are tiered: environment constraints and helper invariants are small, reviewable changes, while RTL edits change the product and require a human-approved diff after the proofs pass. Every accepted repair is versioned and reversible, and the final proof artifacts, traces and invariants, are kept so that a reviewer can re-check them.

## Going deeper

Biere et al., "Bounded Model Checking" (Advances in Computers, 2003), on counterexample traces; the SymbiYosys documentation, on base-case and induction traces.

problems.q:
The trace shows an input sequence that the interface spec forbids. What is the right diagnosis?

A) A missing environment assumption, not a design bug

B) A timing violation

C) A solver error

D) A design bug in the receiver
problems.a: A missing environment assumption, not a design bug
problems.e: Counterexamples outside the legal environment point to under-constrained inputs.

problems.q:
The counterexample comes from the induction step, not the base case. How should the agent read it?

A) As a vacuous result

B) As a reset bug

C) As proof that the RTL is wrong

D) As a possibly unreachable start state, which may need a helper invariant rather than an RTL change
problems.a: As a possibly unreachable start state, which may need a helper invariant rather than an RTL change
problems.e: Step-case traces start from arbitrary states satisfying the assertions, so they often show a weak property, not a bug.

problems.q:
Why is a BMC counterexample a good input for an agent compared with a failing random simulation?

A) BMC traces skip reset

B) BMC returns a shortest trace, so it contains few irrelevant cycles

C) Random tests never fail

D) BMC traces include the fix
problems.a: BMC returns a shortest trace, so it contains few irrelevant cycles
problems.e: BMC deepens one step at a time, so the first counterexample has minimal length, which simplifies diagnosis.

problems.q:
An agent's fix makes the assertion pass, but a cover for normal traffic becomes unreachable. What happened?

A) The cover is vacuous

B) The fix is correct and covers are irrelevant

C) The fix blocks legitimate behavior, for example by stalling the interface forever

D) The prover failed
problems.a: The fix blocks legitimate behavior, for example by stalling the interface forever
problems.e: Covers detect fixes that satisfy safety by doing nothing.

problems.q:
An agent proposes an RTL fix for a failing assertion. Which check must pass before the fix is shown to a human?

A) The RTL compiles

B) The agent is confident in the fix

C) The failing assertion now holds, and every previously passing assertion and cover still does

D) Only the failing assertion now holds
problems.a: The failing assertion now holds, and every previously passing assertion and cover still does
problems.e: A fix that breaks other properties is a regression; the whole property suite is the differential check.

problems.q:
After the fix, BMC to depth 30 passes but the original bug appeared at depth 14. Is the property proved?

A) No: only an unbounded proof (induction or IC3) establishes it for all depths

B) No, the bug must reappear later

C) Yes, because 30 is larger than 14

D) Yes, BMC is complete beyond twice the bug depth
problems.a: No: only an unbounded proof (induction or IC3) establishes it for all depths
problems.e: Bounded passes are evidence, not proof; the repair loop should end with a full proof where possible.

problems.q:
Why should the repair harness run in a sandbox with the property suite and covers fixed by humans?

A) Sandboxes make solvers faster

B) So the agent cannot pass by editing the checks themselves

C) Covers only run in sandboxes

D) Agents cannot read property files
problems.a: So the agent cannot pass by editing the checks themselves
problems.e: The oracle must be outside the agent's reach; otherwise the easiest path to a pass is to change the oracle.

problems.q:
The agent adds an assume property that rules out the counterexample's input sequence. Under what condition is that legitimate?

A) Always, since assumptions are cheap

B) Only if the interface spec really forbids that sequence and the assumption is checked on the driving block

C) Never

D) Only if the proof gets faster
problems.a: Only if the interface spec really forbids that sequence and the assumption is checked on the driving block
problems.e: Assumptions must be justified by the environment; otherwise they are another way of hiding the bug.

problems.q:
To make a failing assertion pass, an agent changes it from req |-> ##[1:2] ack to req |-> ##[1:200] ack. Is that a fix?

A) Yes, the assertion now passes

B) No: it weakens the specification instead of repairing the design

C) Yes, if the change is small

D) Only if a human approves it
problems.a: No: it weakens the specification instead of repairing the design
problems.e: Editing the property to match the bug hides it; property changes need their own justification against the spec.

label: Formal results as a tool-grounded reward
lesson:
# Formal results as a tool-grounded reward

Formal engines give verdicts that are deterministic and checkable, which makes them attractive as the reward signal when a model is trained, by reinforcement learning, to write RTL fixes, assertions or invariants. The risk is the usual one for tool-grounded rewards: an optimizer finds the cheapest way to make the tool say yes. Designing a formal reward means scoring the strength of the evidence and closing each loophole with another deterministic check.

## Prover outcomes as reward

A prover returns one of a few outcomes: an unbounded proof, a bounded pass up to some depth, a counterexample, or a timeout. A reward should rank them by the strength of the evidence, for example 1 for a full proof, partial credit for a bounded pass, 0 for a counterexample. A timeout must be scored as unknown, distinct from a proof: treating it as a pass rewards producing problems that are hard to check rather than correct ones. Because the verdicts are sound and reproducible, the reward is grounded in ground truth instead of another model's opinion, and it can be re-checked: proofs come with invariants or certificates, counterexamples with replayable traces. Even a zero reward carries information, because the counterexample explains the failure and can be returned to the model as feedback for its next attempt.

## How the reward gets hacked

Every loophole in the checked specification becomes a target. A model rewarded for proved assertions can add assume property (0), a contradictory assumption under which every assertion passes vacuously. It can write trivially true properties such as x == x and collect a reward per property. If the reward counts a pass of BMC to depth 10, it can learn fixes that only delay the bug to cycle 11, exploiting the gap between a fast bounded proxy and the real objective. If it can edit both the RTL and the assertion file, the easiest path to a pass is to weaken or delete the assertion. None of these require malice; they are what optimization pressure finds when the reward measures the tool's answer rather than the property's meaning. Each one has a deterministic countermeasure, which is the next step.

## Designing a robust reward

A robust formal reward composes several checks. Keep the target property suite fixed and outside the policy's edit scope. Require non-vacuity: a cover on each antecedent and a fixed set of reference covers that must stay reachable under any assumptions. Require teeth: a mutation kill rate, so that properties earn credit only if they fail on injected bugs. Score bounded and unbounded results differently and timeouts as unknown. To keep cost down, stage the checks: elaboration and short BMC as cheap filters, full proofs only for candidates that pass them. Every component is itself a target, so each must be computed by a sound tool check, never by a model. Finally, measure the trained model on held-out designs with full proofs and human-reviewed specifications, since the training reward can be overfit while held-out results show whether the skill transfers.

## Going deeper

Amodei, Olah, Steinhardt, Christiano, Schulman and Mane, "Concrete Problems in AI Safety" (2016), on reward hacking; Claessen, "A Coverage Analysis for Safety Property Lists" (FMCAD 2007).

problems.q:
Why is a counterexample trace valuable even when the reward is 0?

A) It proves the property

B) It raises the reward

C) It can be returned to the model as feedback that explains the failure

D) It is discarded
problems.a: It can be returned to the model as feedback that explains the failure
problems.e: Formal engines give rich, specific failure information that can guide the next attempt.

problems.q:
A reward gives 1 for a full proof, 0.3 for passing BMC to depth 20, and 0 for a counterexample. What does the partial credit encode?

A) That depth does not matter

B) That counterexamples are acceptable

C) That BMC and proofs are equivalent

D) That bounded evidence is weaker than an unbounded proof but better than a known failure
problems.a: That bounded evidence is weaker than an unbounded proof but better than a known failure
problems.e: Graded rewards reflect the strength of the evidence each engine provides.

problems.q:
A team trains a model to write RTL fixes, rewarding it when the prover proves the target assertion. What makes the prover a good reward source?

A) It never times out

B) It explains why a fix is wrong in natural language

C) Its verdicts are deterministic and checkable, so the reward is grounded in ground truth

D) It is cheaper than any test
problems.a: Its verdicts are deterministic and checkable, so the reward is grounded in ground truth
problems.e: Tool-grounded rewards come from engines whose answers can be re-checked, unlike scores from another model.

problems.q:
Rewarded for the number of assertions proved, a model writes many properties like x == x. How should the reward be defended?

A) Ignore the property text

B) Lower the timeout

C) Reward more properties

D) Require each property to kill design mutants or to match a reference property, not just to pass
problems.a: Require each property to kill design mutants or to match a reference property, not just to pass
problems.e: Counting passes rewards trivial properties; mutation kill rate measures whether a property constrains behavior.

problems.q:
Rewarded for the number of assertions proved, a model writes many properties like x == x. How should the reward be defended?

A) Reward more properties

B) Ignore the property text

C) Require each property to kill design mutants or to match a reference property, not just to pass

D) Lower the timeout
problems.a: Require each property to kill design mutants or to match a reference property, not just to pass
problems.e: Counting passes rewards trivial properties; mutation kill rate measures whether a property constrains behavior.

problems.q:
Rewarded for the number of assertions proved, a model writes many properties like x == x. How should the reward be defended?

A) Reward more properties

B) Ignore the property text

C) Lower the timeout

D) Require each property to kill design mutants or to match a reference property, not just to pass
problems.a: Require each property to kill design mutants or to match a reference property, not just to pass
problems.e: Counting passes rewards trivial properties; mutation kill rate measures whether a property constrains behavior.

problems.q:
Which combination makes a formal reward hardest to game?

A) BMC depth alone

B) Pass count alone

C) The model's own confidence

D) A fixed property suite plus non-vacuity covers plus a mutation kill-rate check, with timeouts scored as unknown
problems.a: A fixed property suite plus non-vacuity covers plus a mutation kill-rate check, with timeouts scored as unknown
problems.e: Each component closes one hack: vacuity, trivial properties, bounded proxies and timeouts.

problems.q:
A reward function is updated to penalize vacuous proofs. What else must be re-checked?

A) That the penalty itself is computed by a sound check, such as a cover on each antecedent

B) Only the learning rate

C) That the model is larger

D) Nothing
problems.a: That the penalty itself is computed by a sound check, such as a cover on each antecedent
problems.e: Every reward component is a target for optimization pressure, so each must be grounded in a deterministic tool check.

problems.q:
Solver calls are expensive. How can a training loop keep the reward affordable without opening a gap?

A) Use the model's own judgment as the final score

B) Count compile success as a pass

C) Use cheap checks (elaboration, short BMC) as filters, and spend full proofs only on candidates that pass them

D) Skip proofs entirely
problems.a: Use cheap checks (elaboration, short BMC) as filters, and spend full proofs only on candidates that pass them
problems.e: Staged checking keeps the final reward grounded while most bad candidates are rejected cheaply.

label: Seams and certificates in a formal engine
lesson:
# Seams and certificates in a formal engine

An agent that customizes or extends a formal engine needs to know which parts it may touch. The four-layer model, an immutable core, pluggable policies, parameters and observation hooks, maps cleanly onto SAT solvers and model checkers, and formal engines have an advantage most engines lack: their answers come with certificates that an independent checker can verify. Those certificates are the golden tests that make agent-driven engine changes safe to promote.

## The four layers of a formal engine

In a CDCL SAT solver the immutable core is what soundness depends on: unit propagation, resolution-based conflict analysis, and proof logging. The policy layer holds strategies that cannot affect correctness: the decision heuristic (VSIDS or a variant), the restart schedule (Luby, geometric or dynamic), the clause-deletion policy and phase selection. Parameters tune those policies: decay factors, the restart unit, deletion thresholds. Observation hooks report progress, such as conflicts per second, learned-clause LBD and trail depth. In an IC3 engine the core is the relative-inductiveness query, the frame invariants and the convergence check; the generalization strategy (plain MIC, ctgDown) and obligation ordering are policies; depth limits and time budgets are parameters; frame sizes and clause counts are hooks that let an agent decide whether a run is converging or should be stopped and handed to another engine.

## Which tier a request lands in

Each customer request lands at the smallest tier that can satisfy it. Raising a block's BMC depth from 30 to 60, or changing the restart unit, is Tier 1: configuration, no recompile. A new decision heuristic that prefers variables in the current property's cone of influence is Tier 2: a plug-in at the decision-policy seam, leaving the sound core untouched. A change to how learned clauses are derived is Tier 3: a core edit that touches the correctness argument, so it needs a human-approved diff and full regression, because a mistake there produces wrong UNSAT answers. Customer-specific front-end behavior, such as translating SVA into monitors in a house style, belongs in a plug-in at the input boundary that produces the netlist-plus-property interface every engine already consumes. A seam is well placed when requests of a given kind essentially never need Tier 3.

## Certificates as golden checks

Formal answers can be validated without trusting the engine that produced them. An UNSAT answer from a SAT solver comes with a DRAT proof, checked by an independent proof checker; a counterexample from a model checker is replayed in a separate simulator to confirm that the assertion really fails; an IC3 proof returns an inductive invariant, re-checked with three SAT queries for initiation, consecution and implication of the property. These checks are the golden tests for an engine change: run the regression suite, validate every answer's certificate, and compare run time and solved-instance counts against the baseline. Differential testing between two solvers adds a further check: when they disagree on an instance, validating the SAT model by evaluation and the UNSAT answer by its proof decides which engine is wrong. Changes run sandboxed and are promoted only after every certificate checks.

## Going deeper

Wetzler, Heule and Hunt, "DRAT-trim: Efficient Checking and Trimming Using Expressive Clausal Proofs" (SAT 2014); Brummayer, Lonsing and Biere, "Automated Testing and Debugging of SAT and QBF Solvers" (SAT 2010).

problems.q:
In the four-layer model of a CDCL SAT solver, which component belongs to the immutable core?

A) The VSIDS decay factor

B) Unit propagation and conflict analysis, which must stay sound

C) The restart policy

D) A progress-reporting callback
problems.a: Unit propagation and conflict analysis, which must stay sound
problems.e: Propagation and resolution-based learning define correctness; heuristics and parameters only affect speed.

problems.q:
An agent wants to watch an IC3 run and stop it if frames are not converging. Which layer provides that?

A) Observation hooks that report frame sizes and clause counts

B) The immutable core

C) The parameter layer

D) The proof format
problems.a: Observation hooks that report frame sizes and clause counts
problems.e: Hooks expose live state without letting the observer change the engine's correctness logic.

problems.q:
Where does the restart schedule (Luby versus geometric) of a SAT solver belong?

A) The policy layer: a pluggable strategy that cannot affect soundness

B) The immutable core

C) The observation hooks

D) The proof checker
problems.a: The policy layer: a pluggable strategy that cannot affect soundness
problems.e: Any restart schedule keeps the solver sound; it is a heuristic choice selected from a library.

problems.q:
A customer wants a new decision heuristic that prefers variables from the current property's cone of influence. Which tier is right?

A) No tier: heuristics cannot change

B) Tier 1: change the decay factor

C) Tier 2: a new decision-policy plug-in at the heuristic extension point

D) Tier 3: edit conflict analysis
problems.a: Tier 2: a new decision-policy plug-in at the heuristic extension point
problems.e: A new strategy fits behind the existing decision-heuristic seam without touching the sound core.

problems.q:
A requested change would alter how learned clauses are derived during conflict analysis. Which tier is this, and why?

A) Tier 1, because it is small

B) Tier 3: it touches the core that guarantees soundness, so it needs human approval and full regression

C) Tier 1, because clauses are data

D) Tier 2, because learning is a heuristic
problems.a: Tier 3: it touches the core that guarantees soundness, so it needs human approval and full regression
problems.e: Learned-clause derivation is part of the correctness argument; a mistake there gives wrong UNSAT answers.

problems.q:
Where should the seam sit for customer-specific property preprocessing, such as rewriting SVA into automata in a house style?

A) In the proof checker

B) Inside the SAT solver core

C) In the restart policy

D) A front-end plug-in that produces the same netlist-plus-property interface the engines already consume
problems.a: A front-end plug-in that produces the same netlist-plus-property interface the engines already consume
problems.e: Keeping customization at the input boundary means every engine and certificate checker works unchanged.

problems.q:
A SAT solver change is being promoted. Which golden check confirms its UNSAT answers on the regression suite?
